utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: We can resume the hearing and, Prosecutor, you can continue the hearing of Mr. Suad Mahmutovic, your examination of his testimony, but just before you start, Mr. Mahmutovic, how are you feeling this morning? Did you have a good night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Good. I am pleased to hear that. So, Prosecutor, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, yesterday just before the adjournment you were talking about an incident at the camp which involved your uncle. Today I would ask you to go to another incident that happened at the camp. I would ask you to recall something that happened to a person called Dzevad Saric, another gentleman called Kolarevic and a person from Papraca. Do you remember an incident happening in relation those people? Your Honours, I am on Channel 4, English channel. I am receiving Bosnian and the witness does not appear to be receiving anything.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Channel 6 is English.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: I was speaking to the witness earlier on and he did seem to be able to hear me. Can you hear me? At least the Presiding Judge can hear, so that is one thing. I have no problem listening to my French interpreters at any rate. As far as I am concerned, I would like to say that I am quite satisfied with the situation, but it would be good if everybody was as satisfied as I am!

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The difficulty with you being satisfied is that you cannot hear anybody else. But I was receiving Bosanski on mine. Perhaps I might start again? (To the witness): Mr. Mahmutovic, can you now understand me in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I do not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, can you now understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is perfect now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Can you also hear what I am saying? Can you also hear the Presiding Judge? Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, yesterday afternoon before the adjournment you were telling the Tribunal about an incident that happened to your uncle when you were at the camp. I would now ask you whether you recall an incident involving a number of men, firstly, a man by the name of Dzevad Saric, a man named Kolarevic, and a man from Prapraca? Can you recall an incident at the camp in relation to those men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not quite remember the date, but I know that it was in the month of June when the four of them were brought out. It was about 12 o'clock in the evening at night. It was about midnight. Zoran walked together with Dragan Nikolic, they walked into the hangar. They walked past the people lying on the floor and next to my feet was a man from Prapraca and he hit him with his -- he kicked him. The man raised his head and then he told him: "You can get up." The man answered: "I am old and what can I do for you? What can I do for you at this stage?" The say: "I have to ask you some questions". Ekrem Basic went to get Kolarevic, as ordered by Nikolic. So they took the four of them out the door. The door was ajar. Then they opened the door fully, and they took them outside the hangar to the A electricity pylon. They were mistreated. They were beaten. I cannot tell you how long it took. But then after that we heard a burst of fire, machine gunfire, and then one person screamed and moaned and called for help. But we were all lying on the floor. We did not dare to get up. We were only interested to know who actually had killed the man and I saw it was Dragan Nikolic. When they finished this, the door closed again. Hasim Ferhatovic was taken out to bring them closer to the hangar. The following day they asked Hasim Ferhatovic and his brother Alija and somebody else, whose name I do not remember, and, according to what Hasim Ferhatovic told me when he came back, we asked him: "Where did you, what did you do, you and Alija? Where did you go? What did you do?" He started telling us. He narrated to us. He said, they asked him to put some kind of nylon bags on the heads of these people and they took them outside the camp towards the mountain, to a place called Mracnica. That is where he buried them, this was Hasim Ferhatovic and his brother, Alija. After that maltreatment, brutality continued again performed by Dragan Nikolic. I remember an incident in connection with Dragan when a doctor, a Serbian doctor, came. Dragan closed the windows and the doors of the hangar, and the doctor said: "Dragan, do not close al these opening because you cannot -- open some things so they can breathe." Dragan then said: "You get out of here because you are protecting these balijas". Another detail, perhaps, an elderly woman was there, some old woman, in fact, some 90 years old, Dragan Nikolic asked her: "Would you like to sleep with me so I make you a Serb, another Serb?" And the old woman said: "Listen, but I am old enough to be your mother's mother". He said: "No, no. You can do all kind of things. You are young enough". Apart from my own misery, he actually took me out every day, and one day he took me out from the hangar and he showed me his bayonet and asked me: "Is this sharp?" and I had to say it was not. Then from another pocket he pulled out a penknife and he said: "Is this sharp?" I said: "Yes, it is." He said: "You mother fucking bastard, balija, I will not cut your throat -- I will cut your throat with the blunt bayonet; you will be dying for several days". My hands began to sweat. I began to ask him, I said: "Dragan, please do not torture me, kicking me and so on, but kill me rather". He said: "You, all of you in the hangar together are not worth one bullet". So I was brought to the hangar again. Then I saw Mico Gojgolovic, a Serb, a guard. I asked him to come closer to me and he came. I said: "Mico, please can you do something for me? Can you help me? Dragan wants to kill me". After that he told me, he said: "No problem. We will try to do something for you. If I can do something for you, I will do it". So I was in a great suspense and then Mico came agai and said: "You know what" -----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Mico Gojgolovic that came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Gojgolovic, yes. And he said: "I have done something but you will have to say something". I said: "But what can I say?" He said: "They will take you out in the course of this day. They will ask you: 'Who hit you here?'", and this was Dragan who had hit me and had a great swelling in my face. He says: "When Dragan Nikolic asks you who hit me, I should say that we had been beaten by Veljko Basic and that Veljko Basic was the who does all the beatings". I said: "How can I say when this is not the truth?" He said: "Listen, he is the Serb. He was one who gave weapons to the Muslims. Say so and you will stay alive". So I accepted that. I do not know what time it was when they took me out behind the hangar, and there was Dragan Nikolic with his hands on his back, two hand grenades, a pistol, a bayonet and an automatic submachine gun. He was walking up and down for a few minutes. I had to keep my hands on my back and my head lowered, and he said: "Gazija, who hit you there?" I said: "Veljko Basic". "Who is torturing you in the hangar?" "Veljko Basic" I had to say. Then he took a piece of paper and he said to me literally, I quote: "Whose name is this?" I said: "Mine". "Whose is the second name?" "My brother's". "Whose is the third name?" "Another brother of mine". He said: "Listen to what I am saying to you", said he, "in order to keep you alive, Mico and you are here. We are here. UNPROFOR will come. Television will come They will take pictures of you. When they ask you about me, you say Mr. Captain, Serb Captain, and they will ask you, have I killed somebody, maybe somebody who was trying to escape, nobody else". So I accepted this proposition, and then he asked me: "Are you hungry?" I had never thought about food, being beaten all the time, I could not think about food. So they brought me back to the hangar, and I had to think and I was trying to think what it would mean for Veljko Basic to be accused in such a way when he had not done anything. Anyway, in about a couple of hours, the hangar opened. Dragan Nikolic appeared in the door and said: "Gazija, have we agreed?" I had to get up and I said: "Yes". When this was over, the time came for me to leave, this was the 30th June. The television and UNPROFOR never came. On 30th June buses came and the Sekovici Chetniks from Sekovici. They told us we would be taken for exchange, to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before you go on, who was Veljko Basic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Veljko Basic was in the former Yugoslavia, he was a policeman, but he was retired already. At the time of the war he had been retired, and then he was mobilized again, and I saw Veljko Basic when we were first brought to the camp. He was the one who was writing the lists of people coming into the camp or arriving into the camp. But there was some kind of conflict between them. One day when Veljko Basic said to Dragan: "Dragan, don't take people out, they are not livestock that yo should kill them and torture them". Then Dragan said: "I am God here and as long as I am here, I will take them out, I will kill. I am Karadjic, I am Milosevic, I am everything in this camp". I believe that there was some conflict between them because of me and my brothers, because among the Serbs, among the Chetniks, the Chetniks were not allowed to actually help us. If a Serb tried to help us he was liquidated immediately. They would liquidate a Serb or a Muslim. Unless he followed their dictatorship, their torture, their killing, their shooting, unless he did that, everybody was liquidated. So, anyway when the time came for us to go to Batkovic, the door of the hangar opened and Dragan Nikolic appeared in the doorway with a list of names in his hand, and he began to read the names of people, and as he read he said: "You in the corner, shooting, you will be shot dead, your son is on the other side." So he left some 20 to 30 people in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of these people who were left in the corner that he said would be shot dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not at this moment remember the names. But before my arrival into The Hague, I wrote a list of names because it is difficult for me to remember all the names as I am speaking now, but I know that Cice, a man called Cice, whose name, whose real name, I do not know. That was his nickname. He was tortured every day. Dragan put his boot No. 46 into his mouth. He said: "You wanted to rape my mother, you balija mother fucker". Then he said: "Dragan, I did not. We were neighbours I never done anything", but no pleas would be -- move him, and as he read the names and as he kept the people that he wanted to keep in the camp, at one point a Chetnik from Sekovici came to Dragan and said: "Leave the list. We need you". So Veljko Basic took the list and he said at the door: "Those people that I had put aside for execution, nobody should allow them to leave before I return and they should be in the corner". So, again I think I was lucky when Veljko Basic took over the list, because he actually sent me to Batkovic. Had Dragan Nikolic remained there, there is not a two per cent of a chance for me to be alive. They would have killed me -- quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to Batkovic camp, could you briefly describe the conditions under which you were in that camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I, let me give you some details about the bus being taken to Batkovic, before we came to Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was beating and torture in the bus as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So when we left the hangar from the Susica camp, we boarded the buses and there were four or five people with the Serbian insignia and camps. They made a lineup, a corridor, armed with truncheons and they hit us as we passed by them. They would hit us on the head, on the back and we simply started to run as quick as possible to escape this, and to board the bus as soon as possible. We had to have our head lowered at all times because there were many Serbs sitting on the side, and I was afraid that somebody might recognise me and say that I should be take away. Anyway, I had been shaven, my hair was shaven and they all called me "Ustasha". I had, of course, to keep mum, to keep quiet. In the bus we were asked to sing songs which they taught us, and says -- there was a Bula, a Muslim woman in front of a mosque swearing that she had only ever loved only Serbs and nobody but Serbs. There were four or five people in the front, four or five people in the back, and they would hit as we boarded the bus and continued in the bus. In the bus we had to keep our hands on our back and our heads lowered. When we arrived at the Batkovic camp, we again were "welcomed", in inverted commas, by the Chetniks who were stationed at Batkovic. When our names were called to come off or get off the bus, there was again a corridor or a file of Serb soldiers. The first bus came to a stop. People came out, and they were hit with truncheons, kicked with boots, with rifle butts and so on, and they searched us also. If you had a ring, if you had a watch, if you had any money on you, cigarettes, all of this was taken away. So, we arrived, I cannot tell you exact number of people, but some three to four buses came, possibly up to 200 people, and when we were taken off, we got off the bus, we were searched, as I said. We also had our blankets. There were some 20 of us who had been shaved, heads shaven, whose heads were shaven. One of the Chetniks said: "Well, those whose heads are shaven should leave the group and stand aside", and we had to do this. So we formed a line and he said: "Tak these Ustasha down there to the maize field and shoot them." But one of them, I do not know who, said: "No, do not touch them. They have been shaven only because of the lice. Fuck their mothers". So they returned us to the main group, and the procedure continued. We were asked to go into the hangar, and as we entered the hangar two Serb soldiers were there, again they kicked us, continued to kick us. I also remember very well something I will never forget, that Valjo, a sergeant, met us with a megaphone in his hand. Again the procedure was the same. Two by two, with hands against the wall, so we -- and those who were not yet there had to keep our hands on our backs and heads are lowered. When the whole list was read, he took the megaphone and the list, and then he -- at the entrance to the hangar there was this line of people, so he took the list and read out the names of the people. The names that was read, they would have to go into the hangar and there were six Chetniks, six Serbs, three on one side, three on the other side, of the doorway and they were waiting for us to start entering, and they would hit us before -- until we fainted. With all my pain and suffering and torture, when my name was read I walked -- somebody was being beaten and I managed to pass by without getting hit. But then they -- and I went among the people whose names had already been called earlier. So I stood there like everybody else and then I received a hit with a rifle butt in my back. The pain was very great and he wanted to take me out of the group of people. He want to extricate m out, but then I grabbed another man, another Muslim man, I did not want to be driven out or taken out. Our life later in the camp went on under the Serbian dictatorship where more people were coming from Brcko and Brezovo Polje and Zvornik. Large numbers of men came during the night, sometimes at 2.00, 3 a.m., 2.00, 3 o'clock a.m.. Mostly they brought people by night. There were 1,600 of us in the hangar. They were made for cereals, for corn. There were 1600 people in the hangar which was about 50 metres by 20 metres large. We had to lie down on our stomachs with our hands behind our back, so we could not see if there was any killing or beating behind us, when we wanted to sleep. There were rules; if a Serbian soldier came in, we had to stand up to attention and look down in front of us. We had to greet them in the traditional Serbian royalist greeting. We, Serbs, the question was, good people? We had to say: "Yes". If we had not said that, we would have been maltreated. There were days when they brought hot water, nothing else but hot, warm water, and a small potato. Half a kilogram of bread was cut into 13 or 14 slices. You can imagine how small they were. I also remember one day Zulfo Hadziomerovic was taken out, stripped him down to the waist, by, it was Veljko, not Zoran from Vlasenica but another Zoran and Gligor, and starting beating him, kicking him. He was a man in his early 60s. He was forced to raise one of his hands and: "Look at this sign, he is Ustasha, this is why you are here" which, of course, was not true. I do not quite remember, one or two day after that he died. I also remember that Ferid Zecevic was beaten badly. I think he was from Brcko or from Bijeljina, I am not quite sure -- most likely from Bijeljina. He was beaten by the three of them every day. I think three or four days after that they took him out and made him lie down where he was dying in the worst possible pains. We were taken out to forced labour. My brother Nurija had to go to Brcko, all the way to Brcko. I went to the Mracnica mountain. One day I had to dig trenches. We had to go to the front line. They would say: "Do not worry, you will not be killed by your own men." If I was from Vlasenica I was not made to go to Vlasenica, but the people from Brcko were sent to Vlasenica, and I was sent to places which we did not -- we were not familiar with, Brcko, Bijeljina etc. where everybody had to do what was told -- what they were told to do. We had to carry out all their orders, I spent -- we had a very hard time there until the International Red Cross came. When they realised that the International Red Cross was coming and that the Red Cross was aware of us, they started hiding the minors and older people, 60 years and older, and took them, put them on buses and take them out for a distance of about five or six kilometres to hide them. When they allowed the International Red Cross to register us, I remember clearly they would put Serbs among us so that we they would listen to us, what we would be talking about the visit of the Red Cross. I also remembe that they give us paper and writing utensils to write to our mothers and fathers and family telling where we were. Spajzer Dzemal and Zeljo Vodnik, they wrote on that -- there was a form and there was a question: "Were you captured as a soldier or as a civilian?" and they kept handing out cigarettes to us, "Just say that you were captured as a soldier". I am not sure that people did so. I could not see for myself. When the Red Cross people came they usually stayed about half an hour, one hour. After they left problems started. Now they would tell us: "You are looking for protection. They cannot help you". They started taking our people, two or three or five people, and beat them and kill some of them. I also remember, his name was Isudin, and when he was writing to his parents in Tuzla he said: "I am in the Batkovic camp", he said in his letter. Since the Serbs looked at these and checked all these, inspected these letters, "Who is Isudin?" They said. "It is me". They said: "Get up" and started beating him. "You mother fucker. We are treating you like a prince here and you are writing that you are in a camp. This is not a camp. You are here on a recreation visit and you are on a plantation, enjoying yourself". As time went by the International Red Cross one day asked if they could come in and and talk to us without the Serbs, Serbian guards, being present. Of course, they approved that. Several people from the International Red Cross went into several groups and they asked us what the food was like; "Do they beat you? What are you sleepin on? Are you cold?" They had told us: "You can trust us, and we are people who are only doing humanitarian things and you can say the truth". We were aware of this. They would have a chat with us and ask about hygienic conditions and all the other things. After the Red Cross left they would come back: "Oh, you are complaining of Serbs?" Their strategy was when the International Red Cross came there was good food, there was nice portions and he said: "Don't say that we are making you suffer". Of course, everybody knew it was just humbug, that was humbug, because the food, as soon as they left the food was bad again. When they killed minors and the older people -- when they hit minors and older people, the International Red Cross said: "We know of people, minors and older people, that you are hiding them at such and such a place; they must be released." They released people in Bijelina. They exchanged some of them, deported others. I do not know exactly. We had to stay, of course. When the International Red Cross brought a jacket or a shirt or a pack of cigarettes, then they came running to seize that from us, to take it away from us. The hangar was covered only with a very thin roof and when snow melted it all fell on us, and we were full of lice. It was very cold. I could not take a bath for six months. When they brought plastic sheets for us to protect ourselves and also a little stove to make a fire in and some pots and pans, they came and brought that -- took that away and, of course, we could not say no to that

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave the pots and pans and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The pots and pans and the plastic sheets, it was the International Red Cross who brought them to us to cover the windows with the plastic sheets, so we could have pots and pans and also small stoves so that we can heat some water, that we can use that and do things for ourselves, but they took that away -- all of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took it away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian guards, the soldiers who watched us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you finally released from Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was released from the Batkovic camp on 21st July 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had any lasting psychological or physical problems as a consequence of how you were treated in both Susica and Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly do, both psychological and physical consequences. My hands sweat to this day. I feel pain in my chest. I did not get medical treatment at the time. You know how our conditions are in Bosnia during the war. We live from humanitarian aid. I did not get medical treatment of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went into the camp approximately what weight were you, when you went into Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I went into the camp before I was captured, 65 but then I went down to 30 kilogrammes in three months. In three months I may have eaten not more than half a kilogram of bread. The only thing that saved me was water. I drank a lot of water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your ribs, do you still have difficulty with your ribs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, often, of course I do

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your legs, what happens about your legs, do you have problems with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also I feel pain from the back bone, from the spinal cord, and then I feel shooting pain into my feet. When I stand on my feet, I feel I am not stable enough to stand. I feel a shaking. I have a shaking sensation in my feet. I cannot stand easily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any difficulty sleeping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do have difficulties. I cannot help but have difficulties when I remember, when things, when I see them with my mental eye, what happened to me, to my Muslim people, and also Croats which they also torture. I feel pity for everybody. Every human being who has a soul to me is worthy of pity if he or she suffers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you lose personal and real property, real estate property, as a result of what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I lost my property, certainly. I lost my house, my furniture, two cargo trucks and my own shop. But let me tell you one more thing: When they took me to SUP, to the police station, I begged them, I begged Ljuban Stanisic: "Please do not arrest me. I will sign, I will give away my property. Let me leave the town". "You are" -- "No, it does not work because this is Serbian land; it belongs to us anyhow. You have no right to live here".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Let me ask my fellow colleagues if they have any questions. Please go ahead, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. (To the witness): Mr. Mahmutovic, could you hear or see whether Dragan Nikolic mistreated the women and children who were a Susica camp at the same time you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I could. Let me tell you something. I could see everything exactly because those of us who were beaten, we had to be next to the door. We were ordered to be there, so they would not have to look for us. They said: "I am a gentleman for you and I am not going to look for you." We had a place assigned to us and we had to wait at that place all the time. So, I had an excellent survey, a view of everything, because the women were next to some chests with ammunition. I remember one evening, I cannot remember the names of those girls, I think they were from Vlasenica, they were from Vlasenica, but they were young girls of 18 and 20 years old. They were taken out by Dragan. I cannot tell you exactly how long they stayed out, but maybe two or three hours. What he had done, I did not see. If he had done something they were not allowed to say anything because otherwise they would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, you mentioned a very important sentence. What do you think motivated their attitude against you and against your other, let us say, friends around you? What was the main reason for this persecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was the reason? Is that the question? Let me tell you something. Among Serbs, whether they are from Montenegro or from Serbia or from Bosnia, there is only one reason. It is because we are Muslims, we are balijas, which is a derogatory terms for Bosnian Muslims, an nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: "Balija", what would be the English term for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a derogatory term for Muslims. Yes, I am a national -- I am a Muslim by nationality. The Serbs should translate that. That is a derogatory term used of Bosnian Muslims to refer to Bosnian Muslims, a very derogatory term.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Mr. Prosecutor, I am looking towards you, I would like to know what the translation is. I understand the witness's answer, but it would be good for the Tribunal to have a specific translation. I can understand that the witness may be reluctant to say what it is but, Prosecutor, would you be so good?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would your Honour excuse me a moment? Yes, it is like a racist term, as people might refer to people of black colour by a racist terms or people from different nationalities in a racist way. That is about the best explanation. But, your Honour, I will make some further enquiries and see if I can get a better explanation than that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Fine. Thank you, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned also that when you were arrested you told them: "Take my land and everything and leave me" and they told you: "You have no right to live here". Was this applied to all of you or was it a special case in which you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, it applied it all of us. There was no difference among Muslims. People used to give 50,000 German marks, their gold, their property, thei valuables. If you had given them the entire Bosnia, you had to give it away anyhow because this is Serbian land. "You are descended from Serbs. It is all Serbian anyhow". It was hard to believe things changed overnight as if we had not lived together at all, and although we had lived together for centuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the people who were in the camps some were chosen to be executed and punished. Was there a specific reason for this choice? What determined the choice of the people who were put aside for torture and execution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prominent people were chosen and selected, rich people, educated people, industrious people. They followed a logic of their own. They wanted to liquidate the best Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned they called you "balija". Was there any other derogatory insults or description of you which were used and what did it imply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The most frequent was "balija" but some of them would also call us "Turk". "This is not Turkey, this is Serbian land".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Mr. Mahmutovic , I have two questions I would like to put to you: Do you have an idea or did you manage to see what your guards were doing, Dragan Nikolic in the course of the day or in the course of the evening, how did they live? Did you see what conditions they were living in? Could you give us just a bit of information on that score?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me try to explain. Before the aggression, they did not live as well as they lived during the time of the aggression because they actually robbed Muslim houses an they became richer. What they did during the day is this, during the day they would be picking Muslims in the town, in the surrounding villages. Dragan Nikolic was the main organiser and the slaughterer would meet the Muslims when they were brought to the camp. They would be searched, their money would be taken away from them. So they lived well, I would say. Dragan Nikolic was the one who planned all the action, who planned all executions, and he, I think, knew what he was doing. He had the task assigned to him as to how many Muslims to kill, how many women to have raped, where they should be buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are your feelings now two years after these events, Mr. Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How I feel? It is hard to tell. I feel threatened. I feel cheated. I had never thought, because we used to eat and drink together, I am 41 years old, I could never believe in my life that we who live together, who grew up together, went to school together, they would be visiting us for our festivities, inviting us to their festivities, that all of a sudden they became criminals as if we had come from Bangladesh, from the jungle. I do not know how, what expression to use. No matter what you call me, they would not -- the Serb, whatever swear word I used, this would be like giving them two week descriptions. They hated the Muslims, they hated the Croats, they hated everybody but Serbs. You see, they are Serbian soldiers who robed Muslims, who pillaged the Muslim villages, taking away tractors, lorries and so on. This was usually the lower class of Serbs who did this. Onc the situation calmed down, once you rob a house, you robbed the house, there is nothing more to rob after that. So then they knew who to send for these -- on these looting expeditions. The Serb who took the tractor had to give the tractor to Dragan Nikolic who gave orders. So they actually took the property from their local Serbs. So there was only a group of Chetniks, extremists, although they were all Chetniks, but some of them made more evil and others made less evil of crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you see the future? Do you have an idea what you are going to be doing in the future, whether you are going to be going back to your village? You must talk about these things with your friends, with your fellow survivors; could you tell us briefly how you foresee the future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me try to explain. My chances for return are minimal, because, look, the criminal Karadzic speaks all the time in the same words: "This is Serbian land; this is our land". Of course, I would like to go back but I believe (and I feel personally) that we cannot live any more with those Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Mr. Mahmutovic, we have taken note of your testimony. The Tribunal thanks you. We do thank you and would ask you to go on pondering these matters and hope that you can do so with some piece of mind. Is there something you wanted to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I would like to say something. I am glad I came to this High Tribunal. I am glad for myself and for my people. I think that Dragan Nikolic should know that I am alive, that I am alive, that my brothers are alive an that he could not kill us. That is all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Thank you. Mr. Prosecutor, would you accompany the witness? Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, I have spoken to the next witness that we had planned to call this morning. This witness has told me that he would request that the order for non-disclosure that applies to him as to other witnesses remain in place. He has certain fears. He says that he has no objection at all to giving his evidence with the television arranged in such a way that his face is not clearly seen. He would prefer if his name was not referred to. If your Honours are minded to keep in place the order in respect of this witness, except for those modifications, then it would be my intention to refer to him by the number that has been allocated to his statement. I understand your Honours have been provided with a list of the numbers of each statement. His statement number is 7.5. Your Honours, I understand that it takes a little moment to set the court up appropriately so that this could happen, so should your Honours be minded to maintain the order in respect of this witness, then I think it would be appropriate if your Honours were to adjourn for a moment, simply to permit the court to be arranged in such a way to facilitate the taking of this evidence under these conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Let me quickly consult my colleagues Mr. Prosecutor, we are going to proceed as you suggested. Accordingly, I will ask the Registrar to take note of your request and the request by the witness. Just to remind everyone, including myself, we will not refer to him by name but using the number you have referred to, but the best would be not to use any name or number. But I would ask the Registrar to draw up an order and to take note in the minutes of this hearing of the partial amendment so that the identification, the address etc., will not be disclosed and that the witness 7.5 will not have his face shown. So we will now make the technical arrangements in the course of the adjournment. The Registrar has something to tell me but, normally, I think we should be able to resume at 11.15. Yes, so we will keep the order and we are going to add to it the fact that the witness's face will not be shown. We are going to have the technical services make the appropriate arrangements. So, by your leave, we would resume at 11.15. Is that agreeable to you? The session is adjourned. (Short Adjournment) (11.15 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, I will call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Counsel for the Prosecution, the floor is yours. Kindly introduce the next witness. I would like to recall that regarding this witness the Tribunal has just adopted an order which maintains, which confirms and which amplifies the concealing not only of these elements of identification but also to meet the wish which has bee expressed by this witness that his face be also completely concealed. I would like, therefore, to be totally assured through the Registrar, and on the basis of guarantees from the technical services, that everything has been done to ensure that on the basis of the witness's request, which has gone through the Registrar and accepted by the Tribunal, that all necessary measures have been taken to fulfil the wishes of the witness. Registrar, is there any problem? Apparently not. Let me now say for the benefit of the public and other people involved in this hearing that in order to complete the concealment of the face, I, together with my colleagues, have agreed that we, temporarily speaking, would find it necessary to cover the left side of the room. But as soon as the witness has been shown in and is comfortably seated, we can then remove the screen and then we can begin the examination based on the questions from the counsel for the Prosecution. So, sir, would you like to introduce or show in the next witness? WITNESS NO. 7.5 was called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to stand up, please, sir? Firstly, can you hear me? Can you here me clearly? If you can hear the members of the Tribunal clearly we can now lift the screen, because now the witness is seated in such a way that nobody in the public gallery can see his face and the video services will ensure that the face of the witness is concealed. So, sir, firstly, would be kind enough to stand u and read out the solemn declaration which is written on the document on your desk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Please sit down. You wished to have a specific form of protection. The Prosecutor passed this request on to us. The Tribunal has accepted the request. On this basis you have a total guarantee of receiving this protection. Let me also say to you that on behalf of the International Criminal Tribunal you are here in a place of justice and, therefore, you can give your testimony on the basis of peace of mind and relying on the quite specific protection which you have requested which is also quite legitimate. The Tribunal is very grateful for your presence here and aware of the conditions in which you have arrived. These are very difficult conditions in terms of material as well as psychological considerations. Naturally speaking, if during the course of your testimony you experience any difficulties whatsoever, please do not hesitate to pass these on, to communicate these, to the Tribunal. Counsel for the Prosecution, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (To the witness): Witness, were you born in April 1960?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, on 4th April 1960.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born in the town of Vlasenica

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you by religion a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am. I am a Muslim. . Prior to the outbreak of the hostilities in 1992, were you an employee of the Alpro aluminium factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, yes, I was from 1982 to 1992, from 1982 to 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that factory located near the town or in the town of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The factory was on the outskirts of the town of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do your military service in Pristina in 1981?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. In 1981 I served my military service at Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since that time is it true to say that you have not been involved in or involved with the military but have, in fact, been a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your involvement with the military since 1981?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After 1981 I was once called by Territorial Defence Administration to spend some three days exercising, and after that I had no connection with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, apart from those three days, you had no other involvement with the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is true, I mean, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the early part of 1992 were you involved in any political activities in the town of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was never involved in any kind of politics. I have no interest in that and had no desire to participate nor did I listen to anybody talking politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the establishment of checkpoints by Serbian people, local Serbs and others, in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were three or four checkpoints between -- yo had to pass through three or four checkpoints walking from my home to my factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you know who it was that manned these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The checkpoints were manned by local Serbs, but also there were Serbs from Serbia, the Arkan and Seselj groups, who supported them from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the local Serbs were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The local Serbs were dressed in civilian clothes. They were dressed in civilian clothes and some of them in the camouflage uniforms, such as worn by the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at these checkpoints, were you questioned or required to produce something? Can you tell us what happened when you came upon a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at checkpoint, as I said, between my house and my job I was checked on these checkpoints. They checked for our identity documents. They searched us to search for weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall when Vlasenica was taken over by the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serb authorities took Vlasenica on 21st April 1992, between the 21st and 22nd April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just briefly tell us your recollections of those days and what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those days, with those barricades were erected, people had been brought to the police station, to SUP. They were maltreated. Their houses were searched. There were killings, there were some killings. All of this happened in the town, and I could see this as I went from my hom to my work. Actually, I did nothing else. I only went from home to work. I worked for 12 hours because there were not enough people for all the shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have special authority to travel from your home to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We had my direct -- my manager, Miso Savic, gave the Muslims who remained in the factory -- there were five or six of us -- we were given special passes to move between our factory and our homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the Serbs who manned these checkpoints in and about the town of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them. I knew them because they were mostly my people from Vlasenica, my fellow residents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to name some of the people that you saw manning checkpoints in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can give you some names. At the checkpoint not far from the factory gate there was the two brothers Jokic. One was Danko and his brother Lule. These were the two people who I recognised and saw them regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other Serbian people that you knew manning checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew because they were all people from Vlasenica and the surrounding villages, so I knew them, not always the names, I did not always know the names, but I knew the faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned earlier that you saw troops from Arkan's group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was -- they were dressed in uniforms and had white arm bands, rather, and also the Seselj and Arkan groups had black berets or black caps on their heads

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what role the Arkan and Seselj groups were playing in the takeover of Vlasenica, what role they played?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their role was to man the checkpoints. They were also involved in the looting, killing, maltreatment and they would come. These people were from Serbia. Nobody knew them so they could actually walk into houses without being recognised, so they would take the property and so on, while the local Serbs did it more or less in a concealed 1 fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it that you knew they were from Arkan and Seselj paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I went to work and from work I saw them, and people who were there, they were all saying, they said: "The Seselj group has arm bands on their arms and the Arkan group had black caps or black berets".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How long did you continue working in the Alpro factory for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I continued to work until the 2nd June 1992 at 12 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on the 2nd June 1992 at 12 o'clock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then on that day at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at 12 o'clock on that day I was at home with my family and my brothers. Two men came to fetch us and they said that we should all go to the Susica camp which was not far from my house, some 200 metres from my house, and that they will be interviewed and have to sign loyalty pledge or pledge of allegiance, or something like that. At that point then, as I said, two soldiers came and took us to the camp

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of these two soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first one was Ostoja, known as "Mrki", called "Mrki". I do not know his second name, Ostoja, and I knew him, and the second one was in a police uniform -- I cannot recall the name at this moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to remember what type of uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One was dressed in civilian clothes and the other one was in police uniform, normal police uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed with submachine guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the Susica camp was 200 metres from your home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, about 200 and 300 metres, I cannot be exact about that, but it was very close. I was born in the area so I know the area very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you actually able to see into the camp from your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since they were sheds I could see from my house, but the camp was on the other side of the hill, about 50 metres, but it is on the way, just around the corner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what this particular camp was used for prior to the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war, the camp was used as a storage facility of the territorial defence units, and that is where the camp was later on. It was converted into the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your way to the camp did anything happen to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the way to the camp, I, my brother, my father and my mother were robbed of all our money and jewellery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how much money was taken from you, can yo remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time they took, that was a monthly salary. That was the average money -- an average monthly salary. That is the amount that they took away from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they beat you or physically abuse you or anything of that nature on the way to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they kept beating us. One of the two guards hit me with rifle butts, me and my brother, and my mother started crying and said: "Please do not beat my children", and by that time we arrived at the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the camp what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived at the camp, as I was entering the hangar, I saw about 20 or 30 people and then the door closed behind me, and every five or 10 minutes more people came, more people were brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone at the camp that you recognised when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mostly people from my area, and my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any Serbian people at the camp that you recognised when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian people were guards, and the commander himself, Nikolic Dragan, and his neighbours, Cane, Krune, Vitorovic Milanko. They were guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dragan Nikolic before you arrived at that camp? Had you known him before then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had known Dragan quite well. We had worked together in the same company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the Alpro factory, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position did Dragan Nikolic have in the Alpr factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic was a storage assistant. He was in charge of the storage facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how long had you worked with Dragan Nikolic in the Alpro factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had worked together for about 10 years from the beginning, since the factory was founded -- the factory was founded in 1982 -- and until I was detained we had worked together in the same factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you observed, what were the duties that Dragan Nikolic had at the camp in Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could see, Dragan Nikolic was the leading man, the commander of the camp, because he issued all the orders, who is to be detained, who is to be mistreated in the most brutal way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever see Dragan Nikolic mistreat anybody in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this only on one occasion or did you see it on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him do that twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a person in the camp by the name of Ibro Zekic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything happening to this person Ibro Zekic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw him at the entrance, on the right-hand side of entrance. He was tied there, and he was massacred. His face was all swollen and covered with blood, and he disappeared during one night and where he had been take to, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that had done this to Zekic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember right now, but from the story of other inmates it was Dragan himself who took him out, took him away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the Susica camp, did you also know a person by the name of Durmo Handzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Durmo Handzic. I had known him before that camp where he had worked, but at that moment while that was happening, Durmo was not far from me, about five or 10 metres from where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say what it is that you can remember happened to Durmo Handzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Durmo Handzic, when Dragan came to take him out, he took him out, five or 10 minutes after that we heard stories. It was such silence that we could hear. He was -- Durmo was saying: "I do not know, I do not know", and after that Dragan had brought him back in and the man collapsed on the concrete, and he walked up to him and kept kicking him on his legs and the stomach; the result of which was that after a certain time Durmo kept begging Dragan to kill him, but Dragan said that he was not worth a cigarette butt. So Durmo simply died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also know a person in the camp by the name of Asim Zildzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, if anything, what happened to this person when you were in the camp at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They let us out every day to go to the toilet, so I had a chance to see on my way back from the toilet I saw a man tied to an electric post and I think at that moment he was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the man that was tied to the electric post? Do you know the name of the man that was tied to the electric post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was Asim Zildzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you yourself ever beaten when you were in the camp at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not beat me, but they did beat my brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in the camp for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Susica camp I stayed from the 2nd June until the 28th June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Tribunal the circumstances of how it is that you came to leave the camp in Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken out of the Susica camp on 28th June. Dragan Nikolic came into the camp with a list and told us that we should be calm because we are going to be exchanged. The list came of people that he read out and told us to get on a bus. He specifically said that we were going to be exchanged, but it did not happen because we were taken to another camp, to the Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you on the way from Susica camp to the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the way from the hangar itself to the bus, about 20 metres from the hangar, as we were leaving there were soldiers and they kept hitting us with chains, with spades, with batons. So when we got on the bus they told us to put our heads down, and not to look left or right, not to look sideways where we were going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then Then as we left they forced us to sing Chetnik songs, propaganda songs, all the way to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived at the Batkovic camp, exhausted, hungry, thirsty, panicked, a Serbian soldier read a list of names. As we entered the camp one by one we were again kicked by everybody who was standing on each side of us. So one policeman punched me and knocked out three of my teeth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the circumstances of the stay for the period of time that you stayed in the Batkovic camp, the things that happened to you personally while you were in that camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could say as we were entering the camp we saw a group of people, people from Kalesije. That group had arrived one day earlier and so we were assigned places, and then they came and mistreated us, and a group of 12 soldiers, they found my brother immediately and 12 people started beating him, 12 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment while they were reading my name and telling me where to go I did get about three or four blows -- two or three blows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that the commander came, Drago, and said there would be no problems. They called it "reception facility" because we are civilians and we would be protected there. But, of course, we were treated as prisoners of war later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything else that you would like to tell th Tribunal concerning the stay that you had in Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First days during my stay in Batkovic in the group of 12 people, including my brother, I cannot remember their names because they had nicknames, builder, butcher. There was a man who was an athlete. He was somehow in the way. These people, those 12 people, were beaten about two or three times every day with various hard objects. There was maltreatment galore, and the climate was such in the hangar and it was very hot at the time, it was 35 degrees centigrade, there was not enough air, not enough food, there was a single meal a day until the International Red Cross arrived. I cannot remember the date, but it was the 28th, I think, of August. After their visit our food was increased a little bit. The amount of food that we were given was increased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Batkovic camp for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The total number of days I spent in Batkovic was from the 28th June until the 21st July 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it that you came to be released from Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know, an order came for 400 people, they were Serbian prisoners in Tuzla and 400 of us from the Batkovic camp were exchanged with the Serbs. This was arranged by the International Red Cross. 400 men were taken to Bijeljina and 400 men were taken to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. I would like to turn to my fellow Judges. No questions. Judge Riad, do you have a question? Go right ahead, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that in the camp you were treated a a prisoner of war. Do you understand what that means -- what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a difference between a civilian prisoner and a prisoner of war. I was taken from my home directly together with my family, and I had not been a soldier prior to that time. The people who were exchanged for us, they were all military, military men. They were captured on the frontline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why were you captured, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, this war, it is nothing but ethnic cleansing of Muslims. There should be not a single Muslim living in Bosnia. As an honest civilian, both my father, my mother and my brothers and sisters were all taken out. Up to that day I had worked in the aluminium factory. I had had no problems at all with the police. I just lived my life. It was this confounded war that broke out and brought that trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: I have a question for you in relation to the proceedings against Dragan Nikolic. I would like you to tell us a bit more about the conditions in terms of hygiene in Susica camp of which Dragan Nikolic was the commander. What were the conditions in terms of hygiene in that camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let us start with the hygiene, personal hygiene, at Susica where, as you say, Dragan Nikolic was the commander. Now, during those days we were receiving food brought by their soldiers. This was badly smelling soup. The hygiene was undescribable. The windows were closed. There was high temperature. There were crowds of people. We practicall had no air to breathe. They did not give us water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in that hangar when you were there? Could you give us just a rough idea of how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was there in that hangar there were between 600 and 700 people altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is full time day and night in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do not know, I forget now when I left for Batkovic after 28th June, I do not know how many people were left there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other conditions in respect of hygiene? Could you tell us a bit more about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no hygienic conditions at all at Susica. When we were sleeping on the concrete floor with some straw, there was one meal a day and all the time until the International Red Cross arrived at Batkovic when we were registered as refugees or inmates, the food was -- became a bit better. Then after the Red Cross left we were taken out to work in different villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Red Cross at the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, to the Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I am sorry, I would like to hear more about the conditions when it comes to the toilets, you had to go outside, is that right? There were several of you going to the toilet at the same time? I am sorry to ask you for this information but I do think it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Susica, as I told you, the conditions starting with food and hygiene and the toilet, all this was very bad. There were 700 people and just one toilet. We were taken there in groups and as we walked towards the toilets, w were also being hit and kicked by the Serbs and also as we returned from the toilet. Again, when we were being taken to the camp from the toilet we were again being hit and kicked. As I say, the conditions were miserable. No hygiene whatsoever. I cannot talk about hygiene. During my 26 days there I could not wash or do anything in terms of hygiene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have another question for you. What was Dragan Nikolic like before the war? You saw him over a period of 10 years. What was he like on a day-to-day basis? Did you have good relations? What can you tell us about what Dragan Nikolic was like before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, before the war I can tell you that Dragan Nikolic, I knew him well, and he was also a man who drank a great deal. He socialised with people who did not care much about friendship and so on. So, he was alcoholic, I think, and I did not have much contact with him. I did not socialise with him so much because I just said: "Hello, hi", and that was all the talk that we had together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you think the future holds for you? What are your plans for the coming months and years? Do you think you will return to your village if there is peace? How do you foresee the future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me try to tell you. The question is a difficult one for me because I have gone through all this misery in the camp and so on, and now Vlasenica is now under Serb occupation at the moment and I do not see how I could return there because the fear that I experienced. I woul never dare to go back there for a long time, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your family at present? Are you together? Have you managed to get back together again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My family -- I have a child with me in Belgium. While I was in the camp, my wife managed to get all the papers so I came to Belgium after being released. My other family, my mother died during my time in the camp, and my father and my two brothers are still in Tuzla on the liberated territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Thank you. The Tribunal is very grateful to you and is very aware of the difficulties for you to testify here. I am going to ask that you be shown out but, first, we are going to let down the screen so that you will not be seen until you have left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Thank you. (The witness withdrew) Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: If you care to introduce the next witness and tell us what the conditions are going to be; if we are going to go back to the conditions we had prior to the witness we have just heard or whether we are going to go on in this format.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have spoken to this witness, your Honour, and this witness has indicated that he does not wish to have the order for non-disclosure continued in respect of him. He is happy to give his evidence so that it may be in public and potentially televised. I only ask that the order apply in so far as it relates to his address

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: I would ask the Registrar to make the appropriate changes to the order about partial non-disclosure. So there is the matter of the address, in particular, and please take note of the Prosecutor's request and take note of the Tribunal's reply. So please bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call Nurija Mahmutovic. NURIJA MAHMUTOVIC , called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, first, can you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: You are going to remain standing while you read the solemn declaration that you have been given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Mahmutovic, we have taken note of the conditions under which you have come to testify and, needless to say, the Tribunal has accepted the Prosecution's request. You can testify with your mind at rest before the International Criminal Tribunal. We are quite aware of the difficulties that you might have encountered in coming to testify. If at any moment in time in the course of your testimony you have any difficulties, please speak out about them. So make yourself comfortable and reply, if you would, to the Prosecution's questions. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. (To the witness): Your name is Nurija Mahmutovic

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 8th October 1957 at Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you by religion Islamic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Vlasenica, at Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the most part of your life up until 1992 where did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do your military service in October 1976 until 1978?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political parties in Vlasenica immediately prior to the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice the buildup and activity amongst the Serbian people in the town of Vlasenica prior to the takeover in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed at Milici there was a barracks, and they were practising in the barracks at Milici. There they organised themselves and they came as reservists to Vlasenica, because these people were mostly from Vlasenica, and they went for training to military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about weapons, did you see any weapons distribution going on in and around your town in this period leading up to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. The weapons were brought with the Zastava trucks, in these trucks, and when they came in front of Serbian houses or flats, they would -- and thes house were specially marked as Serb with some object, and they knew that is where they want to deliver the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember now how the houses were marked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, they would place in front of house a vase with flowers, a flower pot, or a crate, or a piece of wood so they recognised. The Muslim houses had nothing in front of them. There were no -- there was nothing in front of the Muslim door. There was nothing. It was empty, so to speak, while the Serbian houses had special objects being placed in front of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These trucks that delivered the weapons were they just ordinary civilian trucks or were they military trucks? Can you tell us from what you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were civilian trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the weapons were collected from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That came from Milici. The weapons came from Milici. It came from the hangar in Susica, because Susica was the depot, military depot, before the war. So that is where they had the weapons, and that was during the peace time. This was -- these were the weapons for the reserve army for the territorial units. So they took all of these weapons and distributed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying they brought weapons from Milici and then stored them in Susica, and then subsequently they then distributed them to Serbian people around the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the way it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the takeover itself of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Rajko Dukic was the main organiser and Zvonko Bajagic called "Vojvoda", so they were gathering in the cafe called the Hunter, Lovac. That was on the outskirt of Vlasenica. That is where they were gathering because Rajko was the manager of the Bauxite Company, he had money and he financed their political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did tensions start to increase in the month of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We saw everything. We saw a Muslim village near Milici in which some 80 people, 84 or 5 people, were killed, Muslims, men, children, women, elderly people. We watched this. We knew about that. We thought, well, Vlasenica was peaceful and calm so we thought it would remain like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of this increasing tension that you saw growing in the town of Vlasenica, did you then do something or go away from Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. We did not want to go anywhere from Vlasenica because they told us: "Don't go anywhere; nobody will touch you in Vlasenica".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall a person by the name of Fehma Alija and Huska Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Alija was my great friend. He had a cottage at Dzamdzici. I had some land there, and we would go together. We would visit each other. We were good friend. He was a barber. He had his own barber shop while his wife was working in the electricity utility company. So we knew each over for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was Dzamdzici from Vlasenica, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say three to three and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see something happen to Fehma Alija and Huska Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a child, a 10 year old boy. I saw Alija and Fehma being killed by Zoran Obrenovic shooting shooting from an armoured personnel carrier. The little boy was riddled with bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zoran Obrenovic, who was shooting from this armoured personnel carrier, did you see what clothes he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was dressed in a camouflage uniform. This was the army camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was with the Serb forces, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the APC, the armed personnel carrier, was the Serbian, I can tell you with full confidence. Obrenovic was a Seselj group member. He had a red beret with the Kokarda, with the Chetnik insignia on his beret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the 10 year old boy, was anyone else killed in that event that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Amir Dzamdzic and his father were also killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at the time when you saw this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
