utterances.text: I was about 100 or 150 metres away from Alija and Fehma when the shooting started. I fell for cover because I could also have got killed. When they stopped shooting, I came to Fehma and Alija and the boy and I buried them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you bury them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not -- I could not bury them deep enough because I was in a hurry because I was afraid I might get shot as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you bury them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I buried them not far from the place where they were killed, some 20 to 50 metres from the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to observe the injuries that these people had suffered when you buried them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Alija and Fehma were, their head, their skull, was open There was no brain. You could not see the brain any more, their skull was destroyed, while the boy, the little boy, as I said, was bullet ridden, and I did not see the body of Fehma and Alija. I did not want to watch so I just put them and buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Alija and Fehma dressed in civilian clothes or in military clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian civilian clothes, of course, civilian. Alija was an elderly plan, probably some 60 or 65, and his wife too. They could not be soldiers or fighters. They were elderly people. They were retired already. So that they could not have anything to do with any resistance or army or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you subsequently arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot hear well? Yes, I was in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances of how it is that you came to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested because I was a Muslim, first of all. Secondly, they wanted to eradicate all the Muslims from Bosnia. One evening they came to my house and started knocking on my door. I refused to open the door because I saw who was coming and I knew that they would kill me. Czar came and broke the door. He entered the house and found me there. He just said: "Come along with us. We will not do any harm to you. You just need to make a statement." I went downstairs and he tied both my feet and my hands and started beating me. They started beating me. The Ducici brothers were there, the Garic brothers were there, Lemi, Kraljevic. They beat me there for abou three hours. I fainted two or three times. When I came round last time I saw I had no teeth in my mouth. They gave me a cigarette. Then Lemi walked up to me and started beating me more. Zoran Obrenovic ordered them not to hit me on the head because that can be -- the scars, that will leave scars on my head. Then Czar took me out to the corridor and unbound me and gave me a cigarette to smoke. We stood there for about 10 minutes. He was holding his submachine gun like this and was talking to me about certain matters. He asked me about my rifle, and then he hit me here at this area with his submachine gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this beating take place in your house or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the police station, in the public security station in Vlasenica, in SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they first took you from the house, then when they got you to the police station that is when they bound your arms and legs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after this beating? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After they had beaten me there, they dumped me into a room two by three metres large. I found Ibro Kavazovic there and his brother Sead. I also found Hadzan Juraldzic and some other people whose names I do not know because I had not met them before. One of them told me that they were from Han Pijesak. They had been beaten like myself every day. They would be taken out from that room and taken to a large room where I was beaten too. When they came back the were all covered with blood. They had scars and bruises on their face and their body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in this room that you said was about 2.5 by three metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There could have been about 20 people, maybe more than 20. I could not count them because I was so traumatized I did not know, I was not really aware of my existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember what sort of ventilation, windows, or whatever they had in this room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no windows. There were bricks. We did not have enough air to breathe. We urinated there. We relieved ourselves there. We could not breathe. That is sort of ventilation that we had; there was no air to breathe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in this particular place, this cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first I spent about five or six days and then they took me to a prison by the court house where a prison had been before the war. I found Esmir Smajlovic there and his brother Mirsad, Drahman Kurjan and Osman, Alihodzic Amir and Jakub. They beat us there every day two or three times. Czar and Goran Viskovic, nicknamed "Vjetar", they would come in the evening, they would take us out to the toilet where they beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They used to beat you in the toilet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they beat you with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With batons, with truncheons, with rifles, with submachine guns, whatever they had in their hands they would use to beat us

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in this prison for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed there, perhaps, 10 or 15 days. Then they took us to the Susica camp, to a hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what you recall about what happened when you arrived at the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived at the Susica camp my brother was there too, my younger brother, and my older brother came with me on that day, and Hasim Ferhatovic told me: "Nurija, can you remember the people that they took out of the prison when you were there?" I told him some of the names, but could I not remember because I did not know all of them. He said: "A bus load of our people went to Visalac near Debelo Brdo, and came back empty and a bulldozer followed, and they were killed there" he said. Ifrek Kavazovic, his brother Sead, Avdo Sarajlic. About 50 people were killed. They were all killed there -- 40, I am sorry, 40 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first arrived at the Susica camp, where were you placed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They placed us in a big hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who placed you in the big hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought there by Czar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you when you first arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent about five or six days there. We were taken out by Dragan Nikolic, myself and two of my brothers. We went out on the left side of the hangar and there was gravel there, and he told us to kneel down on that gravel and put our hands behind our back, behind our head, and he started beating us Dragan ordered me, he kept beating all the three of us and Dragan ordered to me to say: "I like, I love the church better than the mosque", and I answered: "I prefer the mosque to the church. I said you can kill me", and he said: "You mother fucker, how dare you say that?" I said: "Dragan, you can kill me but you will never kill my spirit". Then Goran Tesic, nicknamed "Goce", came to me and hit me 20 times with a handle on my head. Dragan broke my rib here on this side. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the handle? Can you describe the handle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was about one metre from an axe, about this thick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you were taken out with your brothers, what were your brothers' name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mahmutovic Suad and Mahmutovic Mirsad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go out with any other person on that day other than your brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went out with Rasidagic Reuf. He was beaten too. He kept asking him: "Where is your brother?" He looked for his brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you after this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They returned me to the hangar, and I stayed there until the end, until we were taken to Batkovic. One evening he came and called out Handzic Durmo, Zildzic Asim and Smajlovic Mirsad. He took them out next to the A post where we were beaten too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he came", who do you mean by "he"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic. He personally came. He was carrying a submachine gun and ordered for the three of them to g out, Asim, Zildzic, Durmo and Mirsad Smajlovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to those men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic said to Mirsad Smajlovic: "Asim told me that you have a gun, that you have a rifle." And they started beating Mirsad Smajlovic. He said: "Dragan, I have never had a rifle. You are beating me for no reason". They kept beating him there. Then he came back to the hangar. We heard Asim, when they started beating him, he started moaning and sobbing and begging for mercy. He said: "Do not beat me. I have no rifle, no weapons. You know we grew up together in Vlasenica. You know that very well."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they were beating him" do you know who it is that were beating him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic and Djuro Djuric and Tesic and Miso Dosic. They beat him there and we heard his words all the time. After a certain time we heard him lose his voice. He was no longer able to speak. We knew what was going on. Then they started beating Durmo Handzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he lost his voice", that is Asim lost his voice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Asim, Asim, yes. He could no longer speak. His voice was vanishing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Keep going. Then they started to beat Durmo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they beat Durmo and Dragan kept telling him: "Where is the radio station? Where are your sons?" Of course, always cursing him. He says: "I have no radio station and I have not a clue where my sons are. You are beating me for no reason". They kept beating Durmo. We heard hi moan and beg. They beat him with handles, and when they had beat him up, beaten him up, they brought him back in front of the door of the hangar: "Take this manure away", he said, pointing to Durmo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic said. We jumped -- we took Asim. I saw that one of his eyes was knocked out, but I cannot remember which. He had many injuries on the head. Blood was running out of his nose and his mouth and his ears. We placed him there. I put a blanket under him so that we could stand him because it was easier for him that way. When we tried to stand him, he said: "Do not do anything to me. Look what they did to me." Then after about 20 minutes he died there. Durmo Handzic was also brought in by Dragan Nikolic and said: "Take him up". We took him to the far end of the hangar. Durmo spent the night there. He ordered him to take off his jacket and his shirt off and lie down on the concrete floor. He lay down on the floor the whole evening, and when Dragan came the following morning, the man started to halucinate. He said: "Can I go out?" He said: "No, you must not" and he forbad every contact with Durmo. Then Durmo stood up when Dragan was not around, and headed towards a place where his jacket was. He had not walked more than five metres before he collapsed and never got up again. He died at that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Durmo or Asim, were they, to your knowledge, in reasonably good health prior to their coming to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were in good health

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after Durmo collapsed and fell on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He never got up again. He died there. Just as he came to the place where his jacket was he fell down and died. He never got up again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that, after he had died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hasim Ferhatovic took his body out. There was a small shed by the hangar, and Asim had been lying there. They first buried Asim and then Durmo. They took them out in a car owned by a construction company. Asim was buried next to my father's grave and Durmo was buried in the Muslim cemetery. I do not know exactly where the cemetery is. Where his grave is, but I know Asim was buried next to my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person in the camp by the name of Dzevad Saric, another man called Kolarevic, who were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I found them in the camp when I came. One evening Dragan Nikolic came, Kolarevic and Zoran Obrenovic, they all came and they ordered him to get up and go out. I do not know Dragan Nikolic. I do not know the man. He told him also, he commanded him to get up and kicked him and told him to go out. When he did get up one of the soldiers said to the soldier to run towards the fence. I heard rounds of fire outside. I heard yells and sobs outside. That is where they were killed, four men were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those four men again -- I know you do not know all their names, the names that you can remember and where they came from, are you able to tell us

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kolarevic was from a village near Vlasenica maybe four or five kilometres from the town and Dzevad Saric lived on a road in the village of Drum about three or four kilometres from the town. Zildzic, nicknamed "Musa", lived about five or six kilometres from Vlasenica. I knew him but I do not know his name. I do not know this other man, fourth man. I think his surname is Ferhatbegovic, I found out later, but I had no never seen him prior to that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any observations the next morning near the electricity pylon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. As we were going to the toilet we saw puddles of blood. It was -- it could not have been anybody else's blood but theirs. We saw large puddles of blood covered with sand but still blood came out through the sand, and they could not cover it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in the Susica camp did you know of a person with the name Arnaut, Cice Arnaut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know Cice Arnaut. We had lived in Vlasenica together. We had grown up in Vlasenica together. Dragan beat him every day. He had to kneel down on the concrete floor with his hands behind his head, and I saw when Dragan Nikolic pushed his bayonet into his mouth and cursing him, calling him "mother fuck"er and accusing him of raping Dragan's mother, and accusing him of stirring up trouble in Vlasenica. He kept saying: "You can kill me if I am guilty, but I am not guilty of anything."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remember seeing what happened to some of the women that were in the camp at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember Mevla. She was about 80, 85 year old. She could not walk around. She was too fat and she was just old and exhausted. Dragan came in many times into the hangar: "If my brother does not show up I will rape you so I can make a Serb". He ordered Srce -- that was the nickname of another soldier -- that he must marry Mevla and must sleep with her. He often came in the hangar and said that, Dragan Nikolic did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from this lady were there other women in the camp that you saw things happen to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see anything else happen to these women because they were driven -- they were transported to Srpske.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed, I cannot quite remember clearly, I do not remember exactly the date we left, but I stayed 20 or 25 days. I find it difficult to think. You can see that I was hit. I have scars all around, and you can see this scar here. I was beaten, specially in the head. So I have lapses of memory. I am beginning to lose my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from beginning to lose your memory, sometimes do you have problems with your eyesight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot see with this left eye. It is hazy in front of that eye and sometimes I cannot see anything, because I was hit here -- I still have the scar -- and probably that comes from that blow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your eye was working all right prior to then, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had good vision. I have good vision with my right eye now, but I cannot see well with my left eye now. I think I have lost about 70 per cent of vision in this left eye

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it that hit you in the eye that caused you to have this problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When this happened, when I was beaten in SUP, when Czar tied my hands he broke here, here, on the forehead and also knocked out my teeth. They knocked out 12 of my teeth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it that you came to leave? Can you describe the circumstances of your leaving of the Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can describe every detail I think. One day buses started leaving for the Batkovic camp from Susica at intervals of two to three days. People came from Sekovici. There was a man that was called Vukovaras because he had been fighting at Vukovar. So when we were boarding the buses, some 10 to 15 of them would stand on either side of where we had to walk. They had police batons, and as we passed they would hit us and kick us until we entered the bus. As we were entered the bus, as we boarded the bus, we had to lower our heads and they continued to hit us on the back with the batons, all the way to the Batkovic camp. When we came to Batkovic again they prepared a file, two files of soldiers from the bus to the door of the hangar, and as our names were called we had to go into the hangar; we had to go past between two lines, and I was hit badly on the head on that occasion. I fainted also, my brother too. This was all done by Fekret from Braslo Porlay. Jamo known as Spica. Then also Omer, somebody from Doboj. Our own people, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances of your stay when you were in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was bad altogether. They continued to beat us. We di not have much food, and we received a small thin slice of bread once a day; this was supposed to feed us for the whole day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people beaten in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. I know some people, some 12 people, soldiers, were there called special troops, special units or something like that. They hit Amir Berbic. They beat Alija, known as Konjanik, and Fadil Alihodzic known as "Praga", Edo known as Trocijevac; then Nedim Sarcevic known as the green beret, Mirsad Kolarevic, they called him also the green beret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about yourself, were you beaten when you were in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Fikret known as "Pikvic" beat me three to four times for no reason, started hitting me and kicking me with a baton without any reason or any provocation. He did the same to others. He would just say, "You come out", and he would start beating us without telling us why, because he was a captain in the former Yugoslav army, he was a reserve captain, and he had been fighting with the Serbs and was brought to man the guards at the Batkovic hangar. He had special sleeping accommodation, sleeping accommodation with the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever required to go and work in labour when you were in the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, while we were at Batkovic we were sent to do forced labour. If you did not want to work then you would would be beaten more; you would not get food at all. I was sent to Brcko and I spent seven and a half months there. I was digging trenches on a daily basis. Usuall for 72 hours you would be digging without rest, without food, but we were forced to do that. Some of our people then got wounded because this was the battle front. We had no medical assistance. Once you were wounded they would simply throw you into a room and you would be lying there. A man called Usic, he is an American now, he was wounded there and his leg was festered, the wounds were festering, but he received no help, no medical treatment. When we were sent for exchange we were taken back to Batkovic. When we came to Batkovic one of the soldiers started beating me because I had a packet of cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just stopping for a moment and going back to when you were on the frontline, how far with you from the actual enemy lines or the opposition lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, their lines were here and the Bosnian lines were on the opposite side. We had to go in front of them. If there was a mine we actually had to demine the place and then dig trenches. They forced us to do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they give you in order you could demine the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing. We worked in civilian clothes. They would give you a pick axe and a spade and an axe, so you would cut a root or a tree or something, they ordered us to do, while the guards stood behind us with their guns pointed at us. You could not run away of course. You could not smoke. You could not not sit down. You had to dig. Vojvoda actually forced us to dig trenches with our hands because we did not have the tools. They said we should now dig with our hands and they continued to beat us while we were doing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give me some idea of, from time to time, how fa the Bosnian lines were in terms of metres kilometres or whatever from where you were working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Brcko all along the battle line. In some places the distance was 500 metres; in others it was 300 metres; in some places it was a kilometre. Much depended on the configuration of the land and on the actual lines of battle and how they established lines of battle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to tell the Tribunal about your experiences in the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could perhaps say that I expect the criminals to be punished. I think that the world has never seen the kind of crimes that the Chetniks the Serbs committed against us. I would like to say that and thank the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. I would like to tender my fellow Judges. Your Honour, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Nurija Mahmutovic, you mentioned that in a nearby village of Vlasenica there was an extermination of almost the whole village of 80 people. What was the reason of this massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason was very simple; they were Muslims. On that occasion the husband of my cousin was killed and his son, young son. That was at the village of Zaklopaca. This was organised by somebody who I knew by sight but whose name I do not know, but he was a man from Milici who organised all this, because Muslims had lived in that village. The village was predominantly Muslim. There were some Serbs there but not many. They were simply killed because they were Muslims; no other reaso whatsoever. These were mostly elderly people, children and women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no discrimination between children, women and old people? They all were subject to this extermination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They made no distinction, no distinction. They would be killing regardless of whether you were an old man, a child, an adult or whatever. They made no distinction at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there was a truck of 40 people which disappeared and you were told that they were killed. Did this happen often, that they would take people in trucks and they disappeared forever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did happen quite often. You see these people would be taken from the SUP, from the police station, and from the municipal prison. Their names would be called like Avo Sarajlic, Sead Talazovic, his brother Ibro, Muharem Talalovic and his two sons, Mato and Deba. I do not know remember all of the names because on three occasions they called the names and before they were taken their names were checked for three times, and Bato Tesic, when I asked him: "Will Hasim Ferhatovic be exchanged?" he said: "No, this is not an exchange, this is execution." Later it was found Hasim Ferhatovic was called up there to bury some people. He saw the pit where they were buried. He saw blood, together with his brother Alija who accompanied him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are speaking of Alija. Was this Alija who was shot from a truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Alija Ferhatovic I am speaking about. That is the brother of Hasim Ferhatovic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was another case in which Alija, a certain Alija, was shot from a truck; was that a normal -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is Alija Sahimpasic, but he was not on the truck, in that truck which took so 40 people; that was a different incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Alija Sahmipasic was killed from a Browning. He, his wife, Fehma, and a 10 year old son, they were killed at Dzamdzici, killed by Zoran Obrenovic with a Browning pistol, and he was shooting from the armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a common phenomenon that they would shoot people from the carriers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was done. The armoured personnel carrier was on an elevation, elevated hill, and people sitting in the armoured personnel carrier had a good view of the whole village, because they could see very well this was a Muslim village, and Zoran Obrenovic was Seselj, part of Seselj's group, and he actually ordered all the slaughter and killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Mahmutovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Mr. Mahmutovic, I would like to ask you a question. There was also forced labour during the day time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, even I went one day, we had to clean the parks, and some people were sent to work in the maize field, also to corral Muslim livestock, so that that livestock could be then transported into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were at Batkovic, from what I have understood, when you went before the Serbs, that is to say, betwee the two frontlines, I think I understood that there were mines there, and that you were made to go out in front in case there were man mines. Now, if that is right, are there people who stepped on mines and who were killed by them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most people actually were killed by fire, armed weapons fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By fire coming from the Serbs or in the course of clashes between the two sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was difficult to say. You see, they put us there. The Serbs started shooting on the Bosnian army, against the Bosnian army. The Bosnian army returned the fire, and you do not even know who hit you. When you die in a cross fire, you do not know who was actually responsible. There were several people who were wounded that way, Sead, for instance, whose leg, as I told you, had festering wounds and so on; another friend of mine from Vlasenica also was wounded there. There was a man from Bratunac who was wounded, Sirdalia, again wounded in the leg, but you do not know who it was that shot because it was in a cross fire, and we were -- they were shooting at each other and we were between them, so to speak, and we had to work. They actually provoked the Bosnian army so the Bosnian army would return fire and shoot at us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told Dragan Nikolic in Susika that you preferred the mosque to the church; you showed how courageous you are, not just physically but also in moral terms, sticking to your convictions. The question that I would like to put to you: What about the other people in the camp, did the revolt in the same way you did on other occasions or not at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that I was on the list for execution while I was kept in the police station in Vlasenica. They showed me a list of 100 people that were supposed to be executed and I was convinced that they would kill me. That is why I was not afraid. I thought it was better to be killed with a rifle or from -- with a bullet than continuing the suffering, the suffering was too much. But then he said: "You mother fuckers, I will not kill you, I will not shoot you. You will die slowly because the bullets are too expensive for us. Your heads are not worth my cigarette butt". That is the way he said it. He said that a cigarette butt was more valuable than our heads. That is what Dragan Nikolic said to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are your feelings now two years after those events? Hate, vengeance, living somewhere else in the future? How do you see your future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, we have been educated in such a way and brought up in such a way never to hate anybody. We will never hate anybody -- but they hated us always.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: The Tribunal is very grateful to you, Mr. Mahmutovic. We hope you have a good trip back and we do hope you can do your best to find peace of mind within your family. Thank you very much. That concludes the testimony by Mr. Mahmutovic and the clerk will see you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: The session is adjourned. We will meet again at 2.30. (Luncheon adjournment) (2.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Prosecuting counsel, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. With respect to the next witness he has been consulted and he wishes to testify publicly other than his address. So, as with respect to almost all the other witnesses, we would ask that the protective order be lifted with him except for his address.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: The Tribunal notes the request presented by the Office of the Prosecutor. The order is, therefore, lifted apart from the address for the witness. So please tell us the identity of the witness and, first of all, ask him to come in.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: The witness is Mirsad Smajlovic. MIRSAD SMAJLOVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mirsad Smajlovic, first and foremost, can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a little -- just a moment, yes, I can hear you. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, only the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Smajlovic. Mr. Smajlovic, you wish to answer the questions from the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal and thereby give us your testimony during this hearing, and the Tribunal would like to thank you for that. It is aware of the fact it is not easy for you to do this. The Tribunal would like to say to you that you are now at a place of justice. You can give your testimony in a calm of state of mind. It would like to say to you that if you experience any difficulties whatsoever during your testimony, please do not hesitate to tell the Tribunal about that. Madam Prosecutor, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you your Honour. (To the witness): Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Smajlovic Mirsad, born on 29th November in 1959.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, that that makes you 35 years of age ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 36 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- sorry, 36 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war where was your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your employment in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in the company of -- in the furniture factory, "10th August," called "10th August"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you lived in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in Vlasenica in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 23rd April an army came into Vlasenica. That was the Novi Sad Corps from Sekovici region and the local people, local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know it was the Novi Sad Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because I remained in Vlasenica for a long time and I moved around with them. They came to coffee houses and they themselves said that they had come from Novi Sad, that they belonged to the Novi Sad Corps

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say anything else about why they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why are they in Vlasenica -- is that your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing -- I did not have much contact with them. But while I was in coffee house with them I knew that they were members of the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the takeover of Vlasenica did you continue to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I continued to work until the 10th May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any military group or armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of any group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on 10th May such that you stopped your employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they sent me back home. When I went -- came home they had looked for me. My wife told me they had come to take me away. A short time after that they came again and they took me to the Vlasenica SUP, the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Viskovic was there, and Bastah, nicknamed "Car".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these civilians or police officers or soldiers, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were part of the police because they had taken over the SUP and they were working on behalf of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were brought to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interrogated. First, they took me to an office and I was beaten there, and later I was made to make a statement to Stanisic Ljuban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you were beaten can you describe what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me into a room without speaking to me ver much. I know the two of them quite well. They were members of the Novi Sad Corps -- I know that for sure -- and the other two were local men. I do not know their name. I had known them by sight when they used to come to Vlasenica. The four of them beat me. Then later I made a statement to Ljuban Stanisic. He did not maltreat me. He locked me up in the prison and I spent two hours in the prison. Then the door opened, the door of the prison opened. My wife and Ljuban Stanisic were standing at the door. He said I could go home, but I had to bring the rifle that he accused me of owning which I did not own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you spent serving hours in the prison were there other people detained in the prison at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were other people. In one cell there were 15 men. It was two by two metres room and they were practically piled up on top of each other. They had been beaten up. They barely breathed. They were so badly beaten that they were barely alive. I knew those people. They were all from Vlasenica, and they remained behind when I left. There were Serbs lined up along the staircase, on each side of the staircase, and Ljuban was speaking from a landing upstairs: "Let Mirsad go through". But after he had gone back to the office, he told them not to touch me, not to beat me. But when he went to the office he started beating me -- they started beating me. I was holding on to my wife and this is how I went -- got out and went home

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 25th May. On 25th May the seven of us -- the seven of us saw people taking -- people being taken out and never brought back. I was not allowed to move around. I was told I must not leave my house. People were taken out and never brought back. I saw that it was very dangerous. And so my brother, myself and five other people headed towards the free territory in Kladanj. On the way to Kladanj, I was captured in Malo Polje. We were captured there. Halfway to Kladanj they started shooting at us. This was already the army of the Republic of Srpske. I saw them shooting, so we surrendered. We surrendered near the house of Car's father also called Bastah. The old man insisted that we should be shot dead. However, when we came to a hill ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I stop you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- to be executed -----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just go back for a minute? There were seven of you when you were trying to go into free territory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly happened when you surrendered to the Republic of Srpske soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they started shooting, we had some food with us, because we knew we could not get through so quickly. We would -- we knew that the patrols were reinforced and they had been well organised. We threw away all we had on our persons. We saw a couple of them. I was the first one who said: "There was no choice for us, we mus surrender." We came up to them where Car's father was. He ordered for us to be shot dead immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there that you surrendered to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about four or five of them on the road, and later on when they captured us there were maybe about 100 came out of the woods, surrounding woods, later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the father of Car Bhasta wanted to have you shot, how do you know that he wanted to have you shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he said so. He said: "Climb up the hill, and the balijas should all be shot dead".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he speaking to at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was speaking to the people standing next to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, police Golf car -- of the make Golf -- a policeman Drago Planincic came. He said -- my nickname used to be Dule -- he said: "Where are you off to?" He says, can I come back?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, let me go back for a minute. After the father of Car Bhasta directed the soldiers to take you up to the meadow and to shoot you, were you, in fact, moved at all toward the meadow or the hill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They kept standing there and we climbed the hill, but when Drago came he ordered to -- ordered them to take down their rifles and not to do anything to us, and told us to come by his car. Later he asked, as I had said, because my nickname was Dule, he asked me where I was going to. I said I was on my way to Kladanj. "Why are you going there?" he said. I said: "I am trying t flee." "What are you fleeing and who are you fleeing? I do not know whom". I pretended not to know anything about the situation. "I am running away from the army", I said, "from the soldiers". I said: "I do not know; I am running away from your army, my army. I do not know. I just see that people are being taken away and not being brought back. There is no life for me in Vlasenica. I have decided to go to free territory". He used his radio station to call a truck. He loaded us on to the truck. He would not allow anyone to do any harm to us and took us to Han Pijesak. There they put us in a cell, and we stayed in the cell, in the basement, two by two, two in each cell and one was on his own. Later on they started interrogating us. They would take us upstairs one by one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you asked during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked where we were going to, what the situation was like in Vlasenica. They threatened us also. They did not beat us upstairs, I must admit that, but they took out their knives and threatened us. When I came, we went one by one, I was the last one. He said to me, started threatening me. He said: "These six others have confessed everything about the weapons". Of course, I had to invent because we had no weapons. He said: "I am going to cut your throat because the others confessed and I let them free, but I will cut your throat", but I knew he was lying. I just stuck to my own and I did not tell him anything. I just said I was running away and that I wanted to go to free territory

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me back to my cell where we spent the night. They came. They opened the door of the cell, with knives always but, as I said, they did not do anything to us. They frightened us, they maltreated us, they cursed at us, but they did not beat us. However, the following morning a little bus came from Vlasenica owned by the company of Birac. They loaded us on the little bus, and took us, drove us to Vlasenica outside the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away is the place where you were -- excuse my pronunciation -- Han Pijesak, from the town of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 21 kilometres from Vlasenica. When they brought us to this SUP, they opened the door. They started offending us, and since people -- since there were people in the street they did not beat us there. Then Bjelanovic came who grabbed Emir Huremovic and put him in his car and took him to Milici. We did not know what was happening to him, but we discovered that he had taken him to Janja where there were still Muslims living together with Serbs, they continued to live with Serbs for a long time after that. Then he was taken to Bijeljina and was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, when you said a man called out Muremovic, you said a man called -- the man who called them out, was he a police officer or a soldier or who was the person who took him out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in charge in the police. He was the No. 1 man in the police, the real commander. As I said to Emir and I gave a pistol to Emir, Emir did not take it, would no take it, because he was a peaceful man. He worked as a policeman. When they were disarming the SUP, when they had disarmed all Muslim policemen, they did nothing to Emir. Somehow he was fond of Emir. I do not know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you are talking about the time period when they were disarming the SUP, that is before the events you are describing now, is that correct? In other words, when they were disarming the SUP, that was at the time of the takeover; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, at the time of the takeover. Just before the takeover they had disarmed the SUP. In fact, it was part of the takeover. Because they had taken all the companies, the SUP, all Muslim policemen, they had driven them home, forced them to go home and people just escaped as they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us go back to what you were telling us which is, I believe, after they took Huremovic out, what happened to the rest of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The six of us were taken off the bus and put in a prison upstairs from the court house. We were beaten there immediately. They used everything to beat us and they did it at every time of the day and night. They would not let us eat. They beat us about three or four times a day.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Just a moment. Where was this prison? Where were you imprisoned? Could I have the precise location? Was it in the police station? Where was it exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the building, former prison, a former, an old prison, in Vlasenica. That was up the hill from the court house, but they brought us to outside the police station SUP is the same as police station. They had some archives there, some files. That was prepared to be used as a prison. But apart from that, that used to be the local prison.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you say you were beaten was it soldiers or police officers or both or do you know who was beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you asking about names? I was beaten mostly and my other companions who were with me, we were beaten by Goran Viskovic, Dusan Djuric, whom I used to know, and another Djuric, whose first name I do not know, then a certain Tesic, whose name I do not know. They were mostly people from the surrounding area of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if they were soldiers at this time or police officers or do you know if they were in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some of them were in camouflage uniform, others wore police uniforms. They beat us when they got drunk. There was a coffee house, there was a bar near called Eskalibro. When they got drunk, they would come, they would come to the prison, they would beat us at random. They would take us out at any time of the day. They did not give us any food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you kept in a cell when you were at the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were four rooms four detention rooms. There were people who had been detained before we arrived, and we were placed, the six of us were placed, in one cell. As soon as we arrived, we were taken out one by one and at that time they called me. Goran Viskovic, nicknamed "Vjetar", beat me. He took me out and he beat me until I fainted. I had a fracture skull. When I regained consciousness I was in blood. He dumped me into the cell again and I fainted again, and when I came to, I saw that all of my other companions were lying without moving. We could not move, we could not sit or stand, so we are so weak from beating. We were not allowed even to ask for the toilet so we used -- we did all our elementary needs in that room. As soon as you asked to go to the toilet you would be beaten in the corridor, so you were simply suffering and keeping mum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 26th May up to, I think, I left the prison on 16th July, I think. That was the date when we were transferred to the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were in the prison for more than one month if you were there to 16th July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, sorry, from 26th May until 16th June, I said June, or I wanted to say June. So, from 26th May until 16th June, it was in June that we were transferred to Susica. When we came to Susica, we found Dragan Nikolic there. He called us. He called our names. There were about 20 people who were transferred on that occasion to Susica. Dragan Nikolic called a row and told us to go into the camp and to the hangar. Later in the hangar, I saw people lying on the concrete floor exhausted, hungry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Dragan Nikolic read out your names and told you to go into the hangar, did he say anything about who he was or his role at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said: "Now you are in my hands. You know that I am God and the stick. You can go in there but b careful, watch out, what you are doing and I will decide what to do with you." Later we were there lying on the concrete floor. We had no blankets or anything of that kind because we did not take anything from our homes. I had a jacket which I put on the floor to lie on it. Every now and then he would come in, maltreated us, cursed us, until one night he called the names, my brother, the name of my brother, and so he was taken out and beaten, beaten by Dragan, and by Goran Tesic and Ljubinko Dzuric. When they brought him back to the hangar, I crawled to him -- you could not get up and walk because as soon as you did that they said: "You will be killed" -- so I crawled towards my brother, and I asked him: "Who was it that beat you?" He said: "Dragan". He said Dragan in the first place, then Ljubinko Dzuric and Goran Tesic. After that, the next night, the following night, he took out Asim Zildzic and Durmo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Asim Zildzic and Durmo before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Durmo not very well but Asim was my neighbour. So we were next door neighbours, in fact. When they were called, some five to 10 minutes later, Dragan walked in and called me. I came out. I saw Asim and Durmo. There was an A electricity pole or pylon and they were on their knees with hands behind their heads. He said: "Here, Mirsad is coming. Now, Asim, say what you have to say." So again he started hitting them and saying: "Now say what you have to say." This was just a pretext for him, because I do not know that they had ever told him anything about me or against me. Asi seemed to want to say something but he was unable to speak. So Dragan then turned to me and started beating me. He kicked me with his shoes, with the rifle butt and then Dzuric, who was actually from my company, he hit me from the back with a handle, with a handle, with a truncheon, a wooden truncheon, and Goran Tesic also joined in. They all beat me asking me about my rifle. They say that Asim said that I had a rifle, and I said: "I have no rifle, Dragan. Let us go home and if you find a rifle in my home, you can kill me on the spot". I told him. He would not listen. He just continued doing what he was doing until I fainted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dragan Nikolic ever indicate why he thought you had the rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he just asked about it, and he said that we had organised as Muslims, that we had an organisation, the so-called "Mahala" organisation -- "Mahala" is a street. So, when I regained consciousness Asim was lying without moving. I saw him lying on his stomach with his head on the gravel. Durmo was in a similar position. So Dragan hit Asim, kicked Asim a few more times, but Asim did not show much by way of reflexes. He also hit me twice more, kicked me twice more in the back, and told me to go back to the hangar. I could hardly get up. Totally beaten. Then I picked up Durmo, so Durmo and I were just about able to walk. Asim could not walk. As I moved toward the hangar, he started swearing, cursing my mother, calling me back to say -- to take Asim into the hangar as well

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was cursing and told you to bring Asim back to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan was doing all of these things. Dragan Nikolic, all the talk was by him. He was the one who was in charge. So, I did go back totally weak and I could hardly barely lift Asim. I dragged him towards the door. When I came close to the door, Durmo had already entered. They closed the door behind us or the hangar door behind us. Some people joined us soon from the hangar, and we dragged Asim to his position on the concrete floor. Durmo was also already lying on the -- in his position, in his place, while my place was immediately by the door. That is where I was assigned and where I was sleeping. All of this was around midnight. They beat us until 1 o'clock or so. Later on, 2 o'clock, Suad Mahmutovic came to my place and Asim was Suad Mahmutovic's uncle, so they came to me and said "Musad, Asim has died". The following morning nobody dare to tell Dragan that Asim had died. But when he entered a man came to him and said: "Dragan, Asim is gone, dead". He started swearing. He said: "Well, serves him right. You will all end up like him." Later, some two or three or four hours later, he came to me and called me, but I could barely move because of pain, and he ordered me to go and bury, and bury Asim. The undertaker car came. We put Asim in some kind of box. Hasim Ferhatovic was with me and his brother, Alija. So we all went to the cemetery. We dug the grave. Hasim actually was doing most of the digging an his brother because I could barely move from the beating. So we buried Asim, and came back to Susica. After a short while, following our return, Durmo died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Durmo's body after he died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he also was buried. It was not me who did the burying. Hasim Ferhatovic buried Durmo as well without a coffin, just like this. Hasim was ordered to bury him, so they buried him not far from Asim. It was not easy. It was difficult. He would come in. He would maltreat us, beat us. He would close the door for us. They gave us food once a day and the food was mostly rotten food. They did not allow us to go to the toilet, and if you went to the toilet, when we were allowed to the toilet, you had to do everything in one minute. If you do not hurry up and do not finish in one minute, you would be beaten very badly. This is a blood thirsty animal. I think that is the way I can describe him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is a blood thirsty animal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan, Dragan, I think. This is -- this cannot be described, no matter what named adjective I used, I could not think of a word that would describe him properly. He would take a rifle and he would shoot above our heads. You could not move, you could not make a move, a single movement. Then he would come with a submachine gun and shoot bursts of ammunition. One night he came in and took Dzevard Saric and my cousin Galib Smajlovic. There were several women in the hangar and they were all crying, weeping. He beat thes two people in front of the hangar door, and when they were thrown back into the hangar door they were helpless. They were returned totally beaten. They could not eat. We had some bread that we had saved or we got the following day. They could not eat, they could not drink water even. The night after that he came and he I thought that he would take these two again. He did not call Galib Smajlovic but he did call Dzevad Saric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this Dragan Nikolic you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All, everything I am telling you was done by Dragan Nikolic. All these incidents concerned him. So, anyway, he took Dzevard Saric out of the hangar. He beat him for about 15 minutes, and this was quite horrible to listen to, to listen to the cries of pain. He was crying for mercy, crying for help. He was tortured for about 15 minutes and then after that, at the end of that, we heard three shots, and when we heard the fourth shot, that was the end of it. Hasim who was outside saw that first Saric was shot in the legs and with the fourth bullet he was killed. When Nikolic killed him, he ran into the hangar and said: "Ah, ha, you are trying to escape. No, you will not, you will not get out of here. Anyone trying to escape will be killed by myself". I think that was all invented, of course, because nobody tried to escape. But he said: "You will not get out of here." He said: "I cannot shoot at you because you are not worth a cigarette butt. You are worth less than that, let alone a bullet." That night he also took Muharem Kolarevic, and a man from Kalesije, I think the name was Ferhatbegovic, Raci FerhatBegovic, I think, and he killed both of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that you finally left Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question, I am sorry. Ah, yes, now I know. I was taken to Batkovic in June. That was in June, and I was in the first group of people taken to Batkovic. Dragan read my name off the list and when he read the names of myself and my brother, he told us to -- he told us to stay, then considered for a moment or two whether to let us go or not. Eventually, he said: "OK, go, although you do not deserve to be let go." But he circled my brother's name in red and not -- but not my name, and everything that happened in Batkovic later was due to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that he circled your brother's name in red?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because when they were being beaten at Batkovic his name was called, my brother's name, and Berbic, Ahmed Berbic was called, and my brother were called together, Smajlovic and Mirsad, and then they said: "We have a list from Dragan" they said. When Ahmed Berbic was being beaten by the Serb soldiers, they called him the "ripper", and they said: "Of course he is the ripper because Dragan said that and Dragan would not lie". That is what they said. So, obviously it was his doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remained there 14 months -- no, I was in prison for 14 months altogether, 13 of which in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at Batkovic did you do any kind of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were forced to do work. It was compulsory for the first four months, if I remember correctly, until the Re Cross came. Now, before that we were not -- and we were sent to work. Later, when the Red Cross registered us, we were then -- we then started to work. We had to go to the front lines to dig trenches. I also worked mostly in the fields or, rather, I was being sent more than other people, probably. Some 30 to 40 people would be sent as groups to dig trenches -- this was not just a single person -- and we were working all the time. We were worked on a plantation. We were not given food. We were not given water. They also shaved our heads. It was difficult. That is a flat country. It was very hot, and then also they were standing behind us and beating us. You are too weak even to take the weeds, and when you -- if you are weak, you pull a weed and then you fall, and when you fall they start beating you again. This was really awful, I can tell you that, what they did to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you finally released from Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was released on 21st of July. That was a big exchange, one of the big exchanges of prisoners. We were exchanged at Sibosnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back for a minute to when you were first brought to Susica, besides your brother did you ever have any other family members at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have any other family members. It was just myself and my brother. They were the only members of our family to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your wife was never sent to Susica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife was there, but she spent only two days there, and then actually she came to Susica two days before I came They were put on buses, told that they would go to Kladanj, but instead of that they took them to Srpske, and she was at Srpske and Srebrenica and with the child, and before my return from the camp she came from Srebrenica when the children and women were allowed out of Srebrenica. So she came to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your child also at Susica for several days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was together with my wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was your child at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is now 10 years old, so he was six, seven at the time. She is 11 now so she was seven at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your child a son or a daughter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A daughter.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I do not have any additional questions for this witness your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Thank you, madam Prosecutor. Your Honour, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. (To the witness): Mr. Smajlovic, you told us that when you were taken to Susica camp there were women there in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were a couple of women, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them? Were they beaten, mistreated, tortured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you the following. They were provoked. Dragan Nikolic, what can you think when he comes up to a woman who is 85 years old and says he will rape her if his brother does not come back in two hours. Then he would not let her go to the toilet, a woman, 85 years old woman. It is criminal. He is a criminal. If he can say that to an 85 year old woman, you can imagine wha notorious criminal he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He did that personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in front of us when he came in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Smajlovic, you mentioned that they were asking you if you were a member of this resistance movement, Mahala. What was this resistance movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Allegedly, what he had in mind, he thought that we had organised ourselves and that we were armed but that was not true at all. That was only his figment of his imagination, a pretext to beat us and maltreat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The killing of Asim, Durmo, Dzevard, Racid and Muharem, was it done with the presence of Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, most of the events took place in his presence and he committed them. He called the names personally and took out the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a certain reason for their selection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He enjoyed killing people so much, so he could not care less who he would take out. All the people whom he had killed, they were innocent people. He could have killed me, he could have killed another person, but the most important thing to him was to kill. He invented things just to find a pretext to kill a man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smajlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Mr. Smajlovic, I also have one or two questions for you. Did you know Dragan Nikolic before the events occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had known him for a long, long time. I had known him for 20 years. We were pretty close friends. We went to football matches together. We went to Sarajevo, t Belgrade together. We were Partisan Fans, the football team called Partisan Fans, but when this happened, not for a second did he give a sign that we had even met, as if we had never, never spoken or seen each other. That was such a criminal that it cannot be described in ordinary language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Needless to say, you were a bit surprised by this change, when you went together to see a football match, over some 20 years in which you knew Dragan Nikolic, did you have any opportunity to talk politics with him, to discuss the future of your country? Did you have the feeling that he was particularly committed to some political idea or another or had any extremist, nationalist ideas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we socialised, we never discussed politics. I was not interested in politics, and he had never mentioned politics in my presence. However, two years before the war, especially one year before the war, he started avoiding the company of Muslims. He started socialising with the leader of the SDS, of the Serbian democratic party, Rajko Dukic. He started spending time with Rajko Dukic. They went to a coffee house in his car. I could see them in the coffee house owned by Isvonko Bijelgic. What they discussed there, but I am sure it was politics, when they were preparing for that. It is 100 per cent certain if they had not prepared this, this would not have happened. They spent a lot of time in that coffee house and Dragan did not go out with other people, except with Rajko Dukic and his third man in the hierarchy of the SDS leadership. He socialised with him. He spent a lot o time with him and they were preparing a feast for us. They hated us just only because we were Muslims -- just because we had Muslim names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Asim was beaten up, from what I have understood, it was you who picked him up and you buried him subsequently. What did he look like physically? Was he on the verge of death? Were you struck by certain wounds or could you describe somewhat what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He looked like a dead man, but he had injuries on his head. When they brought him back, he was black all over. All his internal organs were beaten. We could just hear a rattle in his voice. His face could not be recognised. It had been so disfigured; you could not tell the mouth from the nose. Inside his body everything was destroyed. He just started a death rattle. People around him started crying for a short time, of course, because he died rather quickly after that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: You have finished, Mr. Smajlovic. Is there anything you would like to say before the International Criminal Tribunal? Do you have anything you would like to add? What are your feelings at present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to thank you and express my wish for this criminal to be punished as severely as possible, and I would finish my statement with that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Thank you very much. Your testimony is finished. We hope that in the coming months and coming years you will find the piece of mind you deserve. Please be so good as to see the witness out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Thank you, your Honour. (The witness withdrew

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Mr. Prosecutor, before introducing the next witness, the tribunal would like to meet you in camera in the room next door, if that is all right with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: The meeting is adjourned for a few minutes. (Adjourned for a short time)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Prosecuting counsel, the floor is yours. Kindly introduce the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. The next witness I have spoken to. He has indicated to me that he is happy to give his evidence in public. He understands that his testimony is being televised. He specifically has requested me to seek protection from the publication of his address. So, in that respect, I would ask your Honours to lift the non-disclosure order in respect of his identification, but leave it in place in so far as it applies to his address.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Yes. In line with your request, Mr. Prosecutor, we will lift this partial non-disclosure order as it refers, in particular, to the address. So for those who are listening to us the same conditions will apply as for the other witnesses who appeared without concealing their face and, of course, all other aspects of protection will be made available to the witness as was done by the Tribunal for other cases. Do you have any other information to give us about the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. I call Hamdija Dzamdzic Your Honours, Mr. Dzamdzic has with him a lawyer that he has consulted. Mr. Dzamdzic understands that his lawyer will be in the public gallery unless, of course, he at any stage wishes to consult with him. HAMDIJA DZAMDZIC, sworn.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzamdzic, can you hear what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Would you be kind enough, please, to read out the solemn declaration which has been given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, only the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Thank you, Mr. Dzamdzic. Kindly be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Mr. Dzamdzic, the Tribunal, as the Prosecutor has just said and his department has just said, is quite aware of the fact, and this is your right, to be accompanied by a lawyer. The Tribunal, the three Judges in front of you, has discussed the place which it should allot to this lawyer. Let me simply remind you at this point that, having consulted your lawyer, we are in a situation governed by a procedure in which the witness makes his testimony alone. All those persons who have appeared before us also appeared on an individual basis. Having said that, it is the concern of the Tribunal that your testimony be not only, of course, a sincere as possible, of course quite simply sincere, no more, no less than that, but also that we can create conditions in which you will feel as muc peace of mind as possible and psychologically secure. Our procedures do not allow space for a lawyer to be given, physical space for a lawyer to be given, to sit with a witness in the courtroom. However, the Tribunal wants you to be able to give your testimony in the best possible conditions. Therefore, we have decided that your lawyer will remain in the public gallery. Quite clearly, if at any time whatsoever during your testimony you feel that you need to be present physically together with your lawyer, then the Tribunal could change its decision. However, at this point the Tribunal would prefer you to give your testimony in conditions similar to all other witnesses who appeared before you. Have you understood that, Mr. Dzamdzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: The Tribunal would like to thank you for coming. As I have just reminded you, you may and can give your testimony safe in the knowledge that you have rights which you have been informed of and guarantees of your safety at as high a level as possible. We know that you are accompanied by a lawyer, that you have come along with this lawyer. Therefore, the conditions have been created whereby you can give the best possible answers to the questions which will be raised by the Office of the Prosecutor. Prosecutor, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Is your full name Hamdija Dzamdzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 16th March, 1949.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until the beginning of 1992 where had you lived for the most part of your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vlasenica, in my street, in the village of Piskavice, 89, No. 89.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Piskavice a suburb, is it, of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a suburb. There is only one cemetery between our part of the town and the rest of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until April 1992 by whom were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was employed by the bauxite mines, and there was also a transportation company, transport company, which was a subdivision of the mine. I was a driver of heavy trucks, 60 tonne trucks, which I drove to Mostar, to the Glinisa factory in Zvornik to Smederevo, to Jajce. I was basically a truck driver.
