I had worked there for a long time, 19 and a half years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Leading up to sort of April 1992 had you sensed a growing tension in the town of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had sensed some tension. Before the war broke out, trucks owned by the JNA drove to villages further away from the town, maybe I am not precise about this in my statement, in my original statement, I did not specify the names of the villages, but they went for military training, but in fact they took ammunition there. They did some shooting. They did manoeuvres. It was about 12 kilometres from the town. They passed by my house. It was the main road They came back. They sang various songs. They had 5 pointed stars. That was the real army, the one that I swore by, that I believed in, before the 21st April, before all the hostilities began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnic background of the people who were in the JNA at this particular time that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the JNA there were representatives of all nationalities, of all nations and nationalities, Serbs, Croats, gypsies-- everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this continue right up until April 1992 this mixture of all nationalities, so far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had done my military service a long time prior to that time in 68 to 69, but I was aware of the fact that everybody joined the army because, we had brotherhood, and nobody had any idea that something bad would happen. Just as I swore today, I also swore, pledged loyalty to my country, to defend it, that we will always be together, that we would do no harm, not even give a bad look to anybody else. That was -- that had been my pledge, my solemn pledge, before the war, as far as I remember. I know that it was that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the month of April 1992, had you seen any other armed Serbian groups other than the JNA in the vicinity of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand you fully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April of 1992 had you seen around the area of Vlasenica, in the district of Vlasenica, other armed Serbian groups other than the JNA itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had. That is true. They used to go to variou bars and coffee houses, but I did walk around the town. They were wearing Chetnik insignia, but I thought they were mad, that they would not -- that a normal person would not dream of wearing that kind of insignia. So, I passed them by without believing that they were serious about that. That had happened before in the previous war, that some individuals who were mentally disturbed or alcoholics. So, I was aware that I lived in a country that was united, that we all lived together, we help each other, defend our country from enemies. I did see them, but I did not pay much attention to them. I even heard some shooting about two or three kilometres from the city, from the town. I was a member of various humanitarian organisations and I used to gather the citizens of all nationalities. I was a member of the socialist alliance and everybody was a member of that alliance. That was a party that had members from all nationalities, and that tried to help everybody in their social problems and especially in communal work related to utilities, and we paid no attention to politics. I did have meetings with this party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people that you saw wearing these white insignia, did you know what that insignia indicated? Did you know what it represented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did know, not only from the media but I had seen films 10 or 15 years before that, about partisans and the kokarda was worn by Chetniks. They were criminals in the war, in the Second World War, who had committed the same crimes that they have committed now. The whole world kne about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you continue working in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had worked until the 21st. I was on my way to work and I was stopped and said: "No, you cannot go to work". My job, my work side was 15 kilometres from Vlasenica. He said: "You cannot go to work; you have to go back home". They said: "We have liberated Vlasenica". I was shocked. I said: "Who did you liberate Vlasenica from? What does that mean?" And they sang. They were drunk, and they were wearing those kokardas. But, however, I came back home. I was so shocked, I kept asking people that I met in the street what was happening. They were all shocked and they were more panicked than I was. They said that the army -- the army was getting ready to cleanse the Muslims in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I tried to find out. The following day, on 22nd April, in 8.30 a bus came by without a licence plate. It was a fat truck from Prevoi, from the Prevoi factory, filled with soldiers, armed soldiers. There was a car in front of them with a megaphone and a voice said that all the citizens should stay in their houses until they come and call their names. The checkpoint will be in front of the house, my brother's, Rasid's house. I felt that I was totally innocent because I had done nothing wrong and I had entertained no bad ideas. So I waited. It was about 9.00. It was about 9 o'clock. I found my brother there. He was also shocked, amazed, and Safet Jahic then Tumbac .....

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It does not matter if ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will remember later on -- Tumbac was his nickname -- and a few other men. They were all amazed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But the soldiers who came in came into the shop. They fired shots into the ceiling, and I was afraid and they started using abusive language, offending our religion and nationality and said: "Give your weapons". Before that he came in an unknown uniform. It was mixed. There were five pointed stars and kokardas. They had camouflage uniforms but the insignia were mixed. So I was -- I became suspicious. So, I came -- after he had shot several shots, he started beating my brother Rasid and then Jahic Safet -- Ahmo is his name; his nickname is Tumbac -- and several other men, but they just -- their turn did not come to be beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they subsequently then collect together a large number of people, a large number of Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. They gathered, they collected people. As I told you earlier, they told us not to leave our homes, then they spread the soldiers around and brought people. Even passers by were collected. Everybody had to show their identification papers and those that were found to be Muslims were then brought there. There was a kind of warehouse depot and -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where was this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was near the shop. Not far from my brother's house because that was a shop, and there was a yard behind that for the keeping of tiles, bricks, cement and various kinds of building materials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were collected together there? How man Muslim people were gathered there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 50 or 60, I do not know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you were all gathered together in that spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they separated us. Some 20 to 25 people were put aside separated, and they said: "You will go to the bus and you will be taken to the Vlasenica police station to make statements". Following the beating of the few people, this was -----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this take place at that spot? Were people beaten before they were put on to the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat them in the warehouse because there was a storage space for flour and such things. So they brought them in one by one. They kicked them, kicked them with their boots, and we could see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten at that spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not because there were too many of us, so to speak, and at one point a command, an order, was issued. The bus, rather, military vehicle arrived. They talked something and said: "Let us take these 20 people, 25 people, into the bus. We will take them to the police station". Those who were detained, the elderly people and women and passers by, were then released to go home, and were told to remain in the house and not to leave their homes all these days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the names of any of the soldiers that were collecting you there at that spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, none of them, practically nobody was known to me. I could only conclude that their accents were Ser Bre, and Bre is a Serbian accent. I would know that they wer people from Serbia. They actually said: "We are the Arkan group, we are the Seselj group". They also sharpened their knives to intimidate people. I was not intimidated. I knew I had nothing to hide, that I was not guilty, but there were insignia, both the red five pointed star of the JNA and the Chetnik insignia, but the uniforms were normal army uniforms. There were also some people, some people with bands around their foreheads and these were the local Serbs then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers that you say were from the ordinary JNA, do you know what Corps they from in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were taken to the police station? What happened to you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even on -- as we drove into the town because, as I told you, there is a cemetery separating our part of the town from the rest of Vlasenica, as we drove, I saw a tank stationed alone side the road and pointing the gun towards our district, towards our village, and everything became clear to me. As soon as we got out, they told us to get off the bus and we were brought to a house, to a solitary confinement cell, some 2 to 1.5 metres in dimension, and there was just one brick was missing to let air in, and there was some 26 people of us to this building, to this room, which had about four square metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were put into this cell, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- not only myself, all 26 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten before you were put into the cell

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was all done very quickly. We came with the bus. The distance was a very short, a kilometre. So that was very short, but there were also some 20 policemen, 25 policemen, on the bus. They were sitting and we had to stand up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about what happened to you when you were in this cell? What did you experience when you were in this cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the cell, when we entered, then they probably negotiated some things. Some 20 minutes they started calling out the names. They called Ramiz Duric who was a lawyer who worked in the Vlasenica hospital. He was the Administrative Secretary of the hospital. He came out and then we heard the screaming and moaning. When he returned to our cell he was spitting blood. He had to urinate and he urinated on the spot because there was no other possibility. We knocked on the door and we said: "Now, what have you done to the man?" and we thought, well, he might be guilty. But then they took him into a car and took him to hospital. This is probably the only case that I know in the war that somebody was taken to hospital, because at that time they did not quite know how to conduct the genocide properly. So they took him to hospital. But they were Serbian, Serbian people from Serbia, judging by their accent, who beat him but also local Serbs were beating him as well. We asked him and he just uttered a few words. He said: "Arkan group, the Arkan soldiers". The way he spoke was very weak. Then they called other people, my brother, for instance, and the rest of us. I will not mention Fardlihajic, Adhojic -- I cannot remember all their names because there were a number of them, but a few of them I can remember, and you might perhaps have to wait a few seconds before I remember all the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is OK. When you were kept captive in this tiny cell were you ever taken out and beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you out and beat you, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People unknown to me. I must say Chetniks. For me, they were Chetniks. They were not soldiers; the soldiers should not be beating me, but they were people I did not know. Those who I knew were beating other people. They did not want to beat me because they knew I knew them. They were my neighbours who were beating other Muslims, not me. So they rotated, so to speak. Those who did not know me beat me and they beat those they did not know. So I could not say tomorrow: "Zoran, you beat me or you did not beat me" and so on. So I think that that was the reason; that is why they rotated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what were you beaten? What did they beat you with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With whatever they had at hand, a chain, truncheon, iron bars, then, perhaps, you know, there are the telephone cables with lead, with lead insulator, and they would hit us with that on the kidneys, and then we would urinate blood after that. This happened also in the camp later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in this cell, this small cell? Approximately, how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let us see. For days, from the 22nd when I was detained, when I was arrested, up to the 2nd June. Then they took us also to the municipal prison next door to the cour house. There were more cells, more cells for prisoners. I had never been there before, but then I saw for the first time so there were some -- my lawyer, I think, would know how many cells there were -- but, anyway, and they would move us. So they would move us from the police station to the prison, then back to the police station. There was some kind of movement and there was interrogation with torture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were taken to the prison where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In prison, as I told you, I stayed in prison. This was all very close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 22nd of April until the 2nd June. On 2nd June they took some of us on a bus. Some people remained. You know, the population was changing. Somebody would come during the night. Somebody would leave during the night. They were beating us and I lost track of all this. This became a kind of daily routine. I was beaten today in the morning, again in the evening because they came, they were drunk, and I did not know them. Those that I knew beat other people who they did not know. This was some funny tactics they had; I do not even know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever beaten in either the small cell or in the prison by anyone that you did know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in the cell there was not enough place in the cell to beat people. He would have to hit me so I could collapse, put me on a chair, tie my hands behind my back. So they needed more room. In that small cell with 25 people, sometimes only 20 people, but that was not enough room fo torture in prison as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the SUP -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, they needed more space to be able to swing -- you cannot do it in a small, compact space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Outside of that cell were you ever beaten by someone that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. Were you then -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Prosecutor, by your leave, we are going to stop now for a break. We will pick up at quarter to 5. (Short Adjournment) (4.45 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzamdzic, can you tell the Tribunal how it is that you came to be transferred to the camp at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not just myself; there were quite a number of people. We were selected in the prison. We were placed on to a bus, and were driven to Susica. In front of us there was a car in which Dragan Bastah was sitting, and he drove and he actually stopped the bus at some point and picked up some more people, some passers by in the street between the prison and Susica. The distance between the prison and Susica is about a kilometre and a half. It was through the town we went. We drove through the town. There were people in the streets. They would stop the bus. They would open the door of the bus and they would be brought into the bus and taken together, picked up and taken with us to the camp, to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that were collected, were they just men or were they men and women, and what was their age

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were mostly men, mostly men, middle aged men, I would say. No, they did not pick up women. This was only the beginning of the opening of the camp on the 2nd of June. So, they first took some middle aged people, up to the age of 50, while the elderly people remained in their homes. They were frightened and they did not dare to go out. But they were later picked up in their homes and they were brought to the camp. But this is another story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first arrived at the camp what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2nd June, that was the time when we were brought there. This was in the morning. I did not tell you perhaps precisely. It was around 8 o'clock, I would say, half past 7. I cannot be very precise. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I do not know remember it correctly, I will not tell you, but basically it was around 8 o'clock or half past 7 on 2nd June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the camp where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we reached the camp the camp was surrounded by barbed wired. I must call it -- I must call it a camp now, but it was actually a storage depot. There were two storage houses or warehouses. One was about 30 metres long and some 17 metres wide. This was the depot of the so-called territorial defence, and the territorial defence kept weapons and ammunition there. But the army then collected the weapons and the ammunition and left empty crates, boxes, some oil cans, empty oil cans, from the oil for the heavy artillery guns. They asked us to clean the concrete so that only the concrete floor was left bare. We moved all of these things to the other warehouse which was the a warehouse for all kinds of things and they told us: "You will sleep in this first warehouse".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were the first people to actually be taken to this camp? You were among the first group of people to be taken to this camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When in these very early days when it was just started, who was in charge of the camp at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man in charge was Veljko Basic. He was a retired policeman and I knew him personally quite well. I cannot say anything bad about him because I swore to tell the truth. He was not a bad man. So, if you needed something you could approach him. That was about three or four days until the 7th. So he would listen to you and he would then allow us to have water; we could go to the toilet. This was just an outhouse. There was grass there and there was -- and we would urinate and defecated in the grass. But this was -- and there was an outhouse. There were guards around the camp, and he said: "Now, you, balija, do not try to escape." But that was the beginning. Basic was there. He kept the lists of names and I must say that that was until the 7th June, until 7th June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on 7th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 7th June, around 11 o'clock, a group of people from the Kalesije Opstina and Sekovici Opstina some 30 kilometres from Vlasenica, they were brought. They had been kept at Sekovici, then moved to a school in Vlasenica and from that school they were transferred on 7th June to Susica camp This was the first time that I saw the person called Dragan, "Jenki". He was a tall man. He with an open machine gun, an unbuttoned shirt. I knew him very -- by sight from before, but I did not know anything about him in any detail. I had known his father, though, who had died previously. So, anyway that was on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dragan Jenki, what was his surname that you saw bring these people here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Jenki", Dragan Nikolic "Jenki". "Jenki" was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His family name was Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he appear to be in charge of this group of people that were brought in on 7th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he actually brought them and I think it was his duty to put them into the camp. But since we were from Vlasenica, he put our Vlasenica group into one part of the building and said: "This is for the other half. The other half would be the other group." So, the Ustasha and balija No. 1 would be those from Vlasenica in one corner, and the Ustasha and balija group (2) would be in the other corner. So they had the list, they must have had the list at school, so they called their names. They probably had probably been brought to Vlasenica on 2nd or 3rd June and were kept in the trade school in the centre of the town and were brought to Susica only on 7th, these people from the other municipality, and he came with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From that day onwards, 7th June onwards, did the command of the camp change

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who then became commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man that I mentioned, Dragan Nikolic "Jenki", he became the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did things then change in the camp in terms of the way people were treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they changed very much, very greatly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way did they change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, it was forbidden for us to go to the toilet or even this outhouse. Also the food, the food -- you would have my picture, you will see when I was only 53 kilogrammes; my lawyer has the photo -- there was no food and we received no food until 4th June. We had not eaten for three full days. Also they started mistreating us. That was the beginning, beatings, taking people out and beating them and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These beatings and so forth, that happened after 7th June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but let me point out, on 3rd of June, Jenki was not there, but some strange, some strange policemen whom I did not know. Veljko Basic was there for several house and then he went after his work. Then they took out Muminovic, his three cousins, a teacher who was married to a Serbian woman, about 2 a.m. and they took them in an unknown direction and they never came back. Jenki was not there at the time. I must say this. It was not done with his presence, in his presence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember one night in the camp something happening to a person called Asim Zildzic and Durmo Handzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well. They slept next to me. Ther may have been about 60 centimetres between us. There was a plump man between us and then there was them. I will never forget that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About midnight -- I am talking about Durmo Zildzic because they affected me more than anything else, the incidents that happened with them -- they had also taken another fellow townsman, but I do not know his surname and he was taken out and brought back. They called their names and took them out. After about an hour we heard blows with dull objects, with blunt objects. There was the guard house there, maybe 10 or 15 metres from there there was firewood piled up with about 10 centimetres in diameter. They used those logs to beat them. It is quiet by night. We could hear every noise, everybody heard. I was not the only one who heard. We heard moans and screams and pleas to stop, to stop the beating, and suddenly the iron door opened and Jenki came in. He told four, he said to four prisoners, "Come out, go out," and they came out and brought two of them in completely without consciousness. Durmo was in the corner and Zildzic was sleeping next to me and Zildzic was sleeping next to me. For about 40 or 45 minutes Hasim Ferhatovic, there were five brothers of Ferhatovic and their father was there, he said Zildzic has died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe what Asim Zildzic looked like when he was brought back into the room? Could you see what his state of condition was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard for me to say, but I will say because I have come here to say, that he was all covered with blood. Hi skull, he was a balding man, you could see it was broken. His eyes were out. His eye sockets were hollow and the eyes were hanging from his sockets. They put him down, the person next to me put him down, and covered him with a blanket. He had difficulty breathing because his blood was choking him, he was choking on his own blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Durmo, did you see what happened to Durmo Handzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Durmo went up and he had a very, very hard time breathing and kept sobbing. The following day he tried to stand up, walked a few steps, fell down, collapsed and we just turned him around and saw that he had died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Nikolic abused the prisoners generally in the camp? Did you make any observations about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do? Tell us what he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only did he beat the prisoners and kick them about with everything, army boots, in the small of the back, he kicked them in the small of the back, even in the genitals, but that is nothing compared to what I am going to say. They would roll up the sleeves and put them on the gravel. Then you had to spread your legs and keep your hands against the wall and then they would kick them. He also beat, especially later he beat Cice a lot. On 30th June, just as I was about to leave, when I managed to leave that camp, not only did he beat him but he forced him to open his mouth and put his bayonet into his mouth. I just turned away. I could not look. I looked away. It was just gruesome

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Cice's name is? Cice is his nickname. What is his other name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arnaut is his surname, Fikret is his real name. I think Fikret is his real name. I am sorry, my concentration is not always perfect. There were so many of them. It is hard to remember the names, but I am hoping to do better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember something happening to a group of men by the names of Dzevard Saric, Musa Zekic, Muharem Kolarevic and Rasid Ferhatbegovic? Do you remember something happening to those men when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember quite well. That happened especially also Saric, he was beaten more than anybody else. He used to work in the municipal administration. He was a quiet person, there was no reason to be persecuted, and yet he Musa and Rasid Ferhatbegovic, he called him from a different kind of Ustasha, from Papraca, and the other three were from Vlasenica. They were killed, all four of them, in one night. That was in the middle June, about the middle of June as far as I can remember. At the time when genocide began to increase it was really, when they were in encouraged in their crimes he must have received certain authorisations. He had a conflict with Ferhatbegovic and he told him: "I am the boss here. You can get out of here."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he", who do you mean by "he"? You keep saying "he"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jenki. Dragan Nikolic nicknamed Jenki.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Dragan Nikolic doing or saying something to the women in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There were two women in the camp from Gradina about two and a half kilometres from the town. That is a big town populated by Muslims. I do not know their names, although I used to go to Gradina, but there was a woman with her daughter. He used to say: "Take off your pants", I just feel ashamed to say, "you should air your genitals". He used to take out her daughter very often, usually early in the evening. He took her outside and she came back sad. Not only had she been weeping, she was shaking. That happened several times. In my statement I said that a woman called Ulma, that she had seen that. She was in the guard house. Cia Zjapsham(?) is her name. She said to me, she asked for a cigarette from me and told me, I said: "What are they doing with that poor woman?" "They take turns, two at a time." Of course you know what that is it is rape. I did not see it myself, but she told me that. She was the one who saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the guard house where this woman was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three women. The one who told me about 7 metres from the hangar. You can see it in on that diagram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this woman stay in the guard house? This woman that you spoke to did she stay in the guard house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She was there and two other women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would was she doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were making coffee. They made coffee for them and they washed the dishes. They had to be there as servants whether they had anything to do with them, but they were there all the time. When they brought food for us then they washed the dishes, and they made coffee for them and they were there

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did they make coffee for? Who did they make coffee for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for Dragan Jenki and the other guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who lived in the guard house where these women stayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who were there, who were doing their duty when the shift came, when their turn came to be there, those who watched us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did Dragan Nikolic stay when he was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that guard house. He was there all the time. He may have stepped out occasionally and would walk, go over to the command which was only one kilometre away, but he had a telephone. He had a good time there. He kept having lambs on the spit. They had excellent food. Of course they had women too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This woman who was a servant in the guard house where Dragan Nikolic sat, she is the one that spoke to you about this other woman that had been taken there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About approximately how old was the woman that had been taken from the hangar to the guard house that this woman spoke to you about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one who was in the camp, this with other woman she was young, she could have been 20 or 22. I would not say that she was older than that, and the one which told me about it she was a little bit older, she was about 32. Cia, the one she saw, what they had done to her, I did not even ask her. I did not even think of asking her. She just offered the information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When she said they were taking turns with this poor girl, who did you understand by the word "they", who did yo understand she was talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards. The guards who were close to Jenki, Dragan Nikolic, who were in the guard house with him, who were under orders to watch us. Jenki was their boss. He was the commander of the camp and they were called guards, but the guards worked in shifts. They happened to be there at the time and they had a place to sleep in the guard house, and some of them did their rounds around the perimeter of the camp. Jenki was of course the boss, but they lived together in the same guard house. Of course we were in the camp locked up in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many guards were there in the camp in total?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They kept changing and I know one guard who was good, who was very good to us, Mico Gojgolovic was his name, who used to let us go to the toilet regardless of the fact that Dragan banned that. He would take money from the prisoners and would buy bread and cigarettes and bring them to us. Mico Gojgolovic, regardless of the fact he is a Serb, I would like to pay a compliment to him because he was really a good man. But when they saw what he had been doing they removed him from the camp because he is not a criminal. He is not blood thirsty and they could not use such people and that is why they took him away from the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many guards used to be involved in guarding the camp? I do not want their names. Just give me a number, if you could, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is wire, a wire fence around the camp. When we went into the toilet, to the toilet maybe there might have bee about six inside and four in the guard house, a total of about 10, between eight and 10. I cannot be precise about that. I did not feel like counting because I kept thinking of what would happen to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you also recall something happening to a person at the camp called Reuf Rasidagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did not tell you about Saric when you asked me, how they killed Saric and his companions. When he took Saric, Zekic, Kolarevic and Rasidagic, Ferhatbegovic from Papraca. They took them out, beat them for a long time and then we could hear a round of fire. Then they came back. Zoran Obrenovic came back. Pajic Sladan from the place called Dragocica and another one whose name I cannot remember. "Look, they have just escaped, so put the covers on the hangar." But Jenki came in, took a gas bomb and he said: "I am going to suffocate you all because it is a waste of ammunition to kill you." The following day the Ruto brothers, Hasim Ruto and his brothers, were called to go out and they were away for about two or three hours. He said: "We have packed them in bags to Seseljevci" and I have shown you on the picture where they buried them. This is one graveyard but there were other mass graves like that, there was another mass grave. He came back without anybody with four soldiers because we could see, it was a big long door, wide door, about six metres wide, and there was also a small door within that big door. Those same men never came back. The following day on 4th June at about 7.30 in the morning we went outside to the toilet. They said: "Wait a little bit." Buses started coming. All the women an children were to pack and go and be perhaps transported further away, somewhere to free territory in Srpska and Kladanj. A bulldozer went about 7.30 and came back at 11.30. There was no need for the bulldozer to do any excavating because our people went digging trenches, so the bulldozer was not needed for trenches because the trenches had been dug out in May already. So the only reason that the bulldozer was taken was to make the mass grave. It is a city bus with the capacity of about 50, 50 passengers. I am sorry, if I have said too much please stop me. As far as Rasidagic is concerned, he was beaten mostly. He is in Switzerland now. You may have been in contact with him. He beat him so badly. He was saved by Jenki's sister because she was a friend of her wives and she asked him to stop beating him. He remained after me and I have heard from him that he was in Tuzla, that he was very, very ill and he is still ill. He was beaten very badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who beat him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jenki.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "Jenki" you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean Dragan Nikolic, yes. Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever beaten by Dragan Nikolic yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever beaten when you were in the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you beaten when you were in the camp? When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat me on 16th and 17th of June, probably 16th o 17th. I do not recall clearly. Sladjan Pajic, but Jenki did not beat me, he only looked down upon me. But he sent me out of the camp. Also then I now have a proteases. I have a metal because I was hit with a rifle butt. I fell. I saw that my leg would not support me. It was shaking. So this was done outside the camp so that nobody could see this, so to have no witnesses. Jenki beat other people, but not me. He also shot above our heads and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 30th June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on 30th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 30th June buses came from Sekovici and together with a Sekovici escort fully armed, also with bands, with insignia, Chetnik insignia, and Veljko Basic appeared. So I felt better. I said there might be a change here. He said: "Now the name that I read should leave, you should leave the hangar and go to the buses". So he read for a long time. I came, when my came I came to him. He said: "Now you are not on my list." But I saw that I was not on the list because all the other people who had come with me had already been read, and I realised I was the next victim because my name was not read. I had some money on me in German marks. Since all the documentation had been taken away from me as from everybody else, I had 100 marks and I put it into my hair, otherwise they looked at my watch, took our passports, identification papers, savings books. They took that from everybody. So you are on the list but you have no document. Also in the fly of my trousers I also had some 50 German marks. I felt if the find one of these pieces they will not find the other. I also had another piece in the side, at the bottom of my trousers. So I thought, well, I have hid it in three places, at least one will survive. So people were standing up, they were leaving and so I came to him, close to him. I took that money. I took that money. There was this pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you come to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basic, to Basic. I am talking about Veljko Basic now, the one who was reading the names, but he did not read my names because I was not on the list. So I now crumpled a bank note and I put it into his pocket. Then he added my name in his own handwriting. Then he read my name. Then everybody started. They moved. He thought there was more money. I gave him a little, a small bank note. He knew he was well-known to be taking bribes but he was a good man otherwise, and I think he saved me in this way, I must say. I was not circled because in the circle, in the list there were people whose names with circled with some kind of signs next to the names and a list accompanied us to Batkovic, but when we came to Batkovic that is another story which I can tell you if you are interested. So everybody whose name was circled was severely beaten without any question. I was lucky enough but at least at that time I was already badly wounded, and so I could not even go to work because my leg was broken. So that was saved. Then the Red Cross came, international doctors, and saved my leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, can you just tell us what you experienced when you were in the camp at Batkovic

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The beatings were regular, commonplace. Different kinds of armies came, different kinds of soldiers, but in Susica there was Jenki and Jenki organised the beatings. But in Batkovic, this was a larger camp and people who were beaten were mainly intellectuals, judges, lawyers, doctors, teachers, these people were very badly beaten. People who arrived on 14th July from Brcko, for instance, until 30th July or early August, until early August, these people had been cleansed totally, which means killed. A Muslim from Brezovo Polje beat them as well. He beat them just as badly as the Serbs. This would be a long story. One could write a whole history of it all. I was lying there because I could not stand. Doctors would come, International Red Cross discovered us on 18th August and they managed to get me out of the camp as a disabled person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you get out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 11th -- there is a document -- on 11th they let me, but we were not released on 11th. The document said 11th but they said we need more people, more balijas for exchange, so I was waiting. I came to Tuzla on 17th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 17th of what month, can you remember, in what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 17th December 1992. That was the date, that was the date when I came to Tuzla, when I was finally free in Tuzla, but my documents say 11th. I have the original documents from Geneva, from the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Judge Odio-Benito, do you have any questions or Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Dzamdzic, you mentioned throughout you statement that when you went to the SUP, which is the police station I suppose, you were gathered there one of the people, Ramiz got hurt and they took him to the hospital. You made a comment, I can even read it, you said: "They took him to the hospital because they did not conduct the genocide properly at the beginning." What did you mean by "not yet properly"? Was there an evolution in their procedure after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, the whole method, the whole method was improved, so to speak. He was taken to hospital just to show that they were humane. This was on the beginning of the war. This was the 22nd, the day when we were first collected and arrested, when the tanks surrounded the city and the army was there and the tanks. I think I said that. The army stationed tanks on the four sides of the city. The army was there and there were also our local Serbs in the town with whom we had lived until yesterday, so to speak. I never knew they would do this to us. They had the Chetnik insignia and the double eagle, double headed eagle. They sang Chetniks songs. They referred to us as Ustasha and balija. On that day even in the camp the guards sang when they were drunk, they sang the Chetnik songs, but as you say for genocide, you see, they were not fully experienced. They did not know how to do it at the beginning, even those who were doing the beating did not how to do the beat properly. They were Serbian people from Serbia. They did not know who was who. They did not know that one was Hamdija, who was Duric, who is a lawyer, who is not a lawyer. They did not know. So they gave him a document and they took him to hospital. Bu they did beat and later they learned how to do it better, because then local people joined in the beating as well, local Serbs, and that then became worse. But, as I say, personally I was not beaten by my local Serbs. I was beaten by people who I did not know like Pajic. I have all the documentation. Jenki did not beat me but he beat other people. I saw him beating other people and I want to say the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned also that when the army came, the army was ready to cleanse the whole city from Muslims, is this statement right, did you say that, when the army came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, they did. They cleansed, yes, they did. They cleansed the whole city. The army helped them. The local Serbs were few. They were not organised to have tanks. They had no tanks. The army, the Novi Sad Corps., had tanks and they blocked the whole of Vlasenica on all sides. That was the regular army with red pointed, five pointed stars, and the guns were pointed in our direction, while the local Serbs in the town they gave the names of people who should be arrested. They helped with the arrests. They eventually even collected old women and thousands of people, thousands of people were affected. I even have some newspaper reports. I know how many people Vlasenica had before the war and how many it has now. I know that many people have passed, have gone through the camps. While I was there, I can only tell you when I was there, but the camp was there after me as well and more people came. This was horrible and this is a horrible experience, I can tell you that. First of all, they call us "balija". We did not eve know why they call us that. Balijas were the shepherds in the mountains, uncivilised people. That is the name they applied to us. They thought we did not know. I understood immediately. I understood that we were actually -- I thought that we had lived in brotherhood and uniity, but then it all dissolved on 22nd April because that was the end of it. Many of my relatives of course suffered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned when you spoke of the bulldozers going for no reason coming back, you affirmed that it was because you were preparing mass graves. Were there any other signs of these mass graves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you, this is my assumption of course, but Hasim Ferhatovic can tell you because he did some burying for smaller groups, for two people, for four people. When Saric and Zekic were killed they had to bury them, but when that bus came that evening it was full of people and then the bus came back empty an hour later, and there was nowhere to go anywhere. There was a mountain, that was a dead end. The road did not lead anywhere. So they might have been taken to dig trenches, but what was the bulldozer, excavator to do, but to build mass graves and then to put earth on top of the bodies. This is my assumption but that was the logical conclusion, and I concluded that and some other people concluded like that. We felt there was no other explanation for this. But the Ferhatovic brothers, they know more than I know because they were there. They know the location. I did not go there. But when they were asked to dig graves there they of course saw more tha I could see. So this was all done within a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who went in the buses, these 50 people, never came back. There was no sign of them after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. Again, as I say, this is my logical conclusion, because there was a man in this bus who was taken out before the bus left. He and the waiter Aldo from Sarajevo Mahudin from Vlasenica, Mufnaga was his nickname. They were taken off that bus which was full of people. We were outside. Veljko Basic was in charge at that time. We were allowed out of the hangar, so the door was open and you could go out, but there was guards all around. You could not escape. So the three people disembarked from the bus. The bus continued on its way and came back alone in an hour. Later Mufnaga was killed by Jenki after my departure from the camp. Then they said that Mufnaga was drunk and that he killed himself, but he could not have got drunk because you could not drink anything in the camp. There was no drink, no alcohol. I think his surname was Fatonic. These three people were taken out of the bus. After that the bus continued on its way. It could not go anywhere. There was another man, a colleague of mine, a driver, he knew people in that bus, Sumacita, Algo Zoralij, Sakip Hadjic, many names which he had never seen after that. They came from prison. The prisons were full, they were packed, and mostly you did not know these people. So they actually moved us from the police station to the municipal prison because there was more room there for the beating. Some people were taken to work. Then they would be taken back to the camp. Tha was the kind of life we had. There was kind of movement, some people worked. I did not work because everybody saw that my leg was broken and that I could not stand. But I must repeat Dragan Nikolic, Jenki, did not beat me but Sladjan Pajic did from Dragazavos near Vlasenica. But I should imagine that Nikolic must have asked him to beat just as my neighbours were beating other people, the people they did not know. So they were unknown people. You should understand this. He did not want to think, ah, well, this was Dragan my neighbour who beat me. No. No, there was somebody else who did not know me, but what they did when I left the camp I do not know, but it was evil. It was all evil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Two points of clarification, Mr. Dzamdzic. Maybe I did not follow you completely clearly. How many women were there at the Susica camp when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a number. I cannot -- there were women and children. They were in the middle because that was before the Papraca group arrived, when that group from the trade school who arrived on 7th, while the women were there already on 2nd in the afternoon, on 2nd in the afternoon, and then on 3rd and on 4th and so on. They came in small groups. There were lots of children and there was a lot of screaming. There were also some elderly people, 70 to 80 years old. So we younger people were kept while these elderly people and women came and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your hangar at Susica during the period of you detention there, on an average basis how many women were there and did they live in exactly the same location as you did and could you answer that question briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That month I was there, roughly one month, there were women for some three to four days, there were up to 200 to 300 women, I cannot tell you exactly. I would say 300 together with the children and so on. They were all grouped in the middle, while we were on the side of the hangar, but on 4th and 5th they started leaving and only two women and one girl which came later, they remained, and they remained in the camp for a long time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Thank you very much. A second episode which I do not think I completely followed. You talked about 100 deutschemarks which you kept. I do not think I followed you very clearly there. So you hung on to 100 deutschemarks following your meeting with the police, having been in the police station, and also you kept it while you were in the camp. How did you hang on to this money? I do not really understand that because I thought everybody was body searched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They searched me, but they did not manage to find the money. I must have been clever than they were, but I had no weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Mr. Dzamdzic, that brings towards the end of your testimonial, but would you like to add anything at all during this appearance at the Tribunal, something which you may have overlooked? Would you like to talk about the feelings which you now experience regarding your past? Would you like to say anything further to th Judges at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could only say specifically as regards Dragan Nikolic, because this is the case, I would only like to know such people would ever live again and that if you ever catch this criminal I would ask you to be very strict with him, if it is proved that he was such a criminal. But for the Batkovic camp I think there is more to tell, and there were also war criminals at Batkovic. I have my list and I have my witnesses who are in Ulm with me, people whose fingers had been cut and nails pulled and so on. I have all of this with full documentation, medical documentation and other documentation. I think that you, your Honours, would be the right court to judge honestly and to bring the criminals to justice. I never thought, I never could imagine what the kind of life it can be. Until a few days before that all started we lived nicely together and then suddenly something happens. The JNA turned into a Chetnik army, into a criminal army, and they committed all kinds of atrocities which were awful to narrate. They called us balija. They used this derogatory name. As I say, the balijas were the forest people living in the mountains, not even the fugitives or the highwaymen were not as bad. So this is a sad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A final question. What are your plans for the future? Are you living together with your family? Do you have any plans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every nine months I must have a medical checkup with the surgeon, with the orthopaedic surgeons at Ulm. I am also working with a psychiatrist every month. The psychiatrist gives me morale encouragement and I find easier to liv that way. When I will be cured I do not know, but I would like to go back to my homeland because I always loved it and I respected it. I respected all the laws. I respected the laws of the army but now I saw what they did, not only in Bosnia, also in Croatia and in other parts of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French]: Mr. Dzamdzic, the Tribunal thanks you for your testimony. We would like to wish you a good journey back to where you have come from. That brings to the end the testimony of Mr. Dzamdzic. I would like to ask the Clerk to show Mr. Dzamdzic out. This is adjourns the hearing for today and we will recommence tomorrow at 10 a.m. (The proceedings adjourned until the following day).
